articles.title: Who is Responsible for the June 20 Police Brutalities in New Delhi?
articles.full_text:
Delhi Police and the Rapid Action Force, which unleashed the violence on student protesters, fall under the direct jurisdiction of Home Minister Amit Shah.
Screenshot of a video of Delhi Police beating protesters with batons in New Delhi, India, June 20, 2026.
Hours after Dharmendra Pradhan, education minister in the Narendra Modi government, stepped down on July 25 under pressure from massive Gen Z protests in New Delhi and other Indian cities, Rahul Gandhi, Congress Party leader and leader of the opposition in the lower house of parliament, sent a letter to Home Minister Amit Shah, seeking accountability for the “barbaric assault on students who were peacefully protesting in Delhi on July 20, 2026.“
Gandhi was referring to the Narendra Modi government’s use of brutal force against unarmed students marching toward the parliament building in New Delhi on July 20.
The leak of question papers for medical entrance exams held nationwide on May 3 triggered a tidal wave of anger and anguish among students across India. Gandhi and the Congress party began holding rallies in various towns and cities demanding accountability from the Modi government.
Then came the protests led by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) from June 6 at Jantar Mantar calling for Pradhan’s resignation. Several went on hunger strikes. The CJP called for a march to parliament on July 20.
As thousands began to march peacefully that day, the Modi government revealed its iron fist in the heart of New Delhi, the Indian capital.
Multiple video clips reveal that Delhi Police and the Rapid Action Force (RAF), a specialized unit of the Central Reserve Police Force, rained batons and fired pellet guns and tear gas on student protesters. In one video, a senior identifiable police officer can be seen slapping a woman student standing nearby. Another video shows a woman being stunned by a shock baton. Protesters have also alleged they were beaten with batons fitted with nails.
At least four people, including a journalist who was covering the protests, have been identified so far with severe pellet injuries. Journalist Vijaita Singh, who accessed the general diary entry by the RAF at 1.24 a.m. on July 20, reported in The Hindu that the RAF’s Deputy Commandant “on the orders of the DCP [Deputy Commissioner of Police]” “fired 55 rounds of non- electrical shell, 15 rounds of electrical shell, five tear smoke granite, two rounds using ballistic cartridges with plastic pellets from an anti-riot gun.”
Incidentally, Delhi Police had denied the use of pellet guns against the students, dismissing reports as “completely false and misleading.”
Importantly, some of those who had wielded batons so freely on protesting students were not in uniform and wore no visible identification. Who were they? RAF personnel who could unleash violence unafraid of being identified? Or supporters of the government?
“As Home Minister, did you approve the use of lethal force, including pellet guns, against students? If not, who did?” Gandhi asked in his letter. “Are the people in plain clothes seen beating students with lathis [batons] police personnel or volunteers? Who authorized their deployment?”
Delhi Police and the RAF fall under the direct jurisdiction of the Union Home Ministry, which Shah heads.
Gandhi’s open letter to the home minister has upped the ante. While the CJP demanded the removal of the education minister, Gandhi and the Congress party are aiming higher — at the home minister himself. They are seeking accountability for the role India’s most powerful minister after Prime Minister Narendra Modi, played in the July 20 violence.
So far, Shah has remained silent on the allegations of the excessive use of force. This is a tacit endorsement of the brutality that was unleashed on students on July 20.
As Rishav Sharma, advocate in the Delhi High Court, pointed out, “Accountability does not end with the constable on the front line; it travels bottom up through the chain of command to those who shape the conditions under which unlawful force becomes possible.“

articles.title: From Hanoi to Manila: Japan’s Updated ‘Free and Open Indo-Pacific’ Takes Shape
articles.full_text:
Tokyo’s Manila diplomacy linked ASEAN security cooperation to a wider Indo-Pacific network stretching to the Pacific Islands.
Japan’s Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu attended the ASEAN-Japan Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in Manila, the Philippines, July 22, 2026.
Japanese Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu’s visit to Manila last week was more than another round of ASEAN diplomacy. It represented one of the clearest public manifestations of Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s updated Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP) strategy, demonstrating how Japan is shifting its engagement with Southeast Asia beyond traditional development assistance toward practical security cooperation.
Takaichi outlined that strategy in a foreign policy speech at Vietnam National University in Hanoi on May 2, marking a decade since the late former Prime Minister Abe Shinzo first proposed the FOIP vision. Takaichi argued that intensifying geopolitical competition, rapid technological innovation, and the rise of the Global South require Indo-Pacific countries to strengthen their “autonomy” and “resilience.” Her updated FOIP strategy identified three priorities: building economic infrastructure for the AI and data age, including resilient energy and critical mineral supply chains; promoting growth through public-private cooperation and shared rules; and expanding security cooperation to preserve regional peace and stability.
Equally important, Takaichi stressed that FOIP complements rather than competes with the ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-Pacific (AOIP). The message was intended to reassure Southeast Asian governments that Japan supports ASEAN-led regional institutions while helping member states strengthen their own strategic autonomy.
Motegi’s diplomacy in Manila put that vision into practice.
At the ASEAN-Japan Foreign Ministers’ Meeting on July 22, he described ASEAN as being “at the core” of Japan’s FOIP vision and pledged closer cooperation in maritime security, economic security, energy resilience, artificial intelligence, and disaster response.
Motegi also said Japan “strongly opposes any unilateral attempts to change the status quo by force or coercion” in the East and South China Seas, language widely understood as directed at China even when Beijing is not named. He further called for any future South China Sea Code of Conduct between China and ASEAN to conform to the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.
The clearest evidence of Japan’s changing approach is Official Security Assistance (OSA), introduced in 2023 to provide defense equipment and infrastructure directly to the armed forces and related organizations of partner countries. Unlike traditional development assistance, OSA is explicitly designed to strengthen recipients’ security and deterrence capabilities.
Recent projects include monitoring and surveillance equipment for the Philippines, a diving support vessel and equipment for ASEAN observer teams in Malaysia, high-speed patrol boats for Indonesia, maritime search-and-rescue equipment for Thailand, and communications equipment and patrol boats for Cambodia. Phnom Penh’s participation is particularly noteworthy, suggesting that even one of Beijing’s closest partners in Southeast Asia sees value in diversifying its external security relationships.
Japan is also moving beyond equipment transfers. Tokyo and Hanoi agreed earlier this month to begin discussions on the possible joint development and production of fast landing craft. The Philippines, meanwhile, remains Japan’s closest regional security partner: during the Manila meetings, Motegi and his Philippine counterpart exchanged diplomatic notes bringing their Acquisition and Cross-Servicing Agreement – signed in January – into force as of August 22, alongside continued radar transfers and expanding joint military exercises.
Tokyo is also trying to connect Southeast Asia with the wider Pacific security architecture. At the third Japan-Pacific Islands Defense Dialogue in February, ASEAN countries participated as observers for the first time. The meeting focused on climate security, disaster relief, and maritime resilience, but it was also shaped by concern over China’s expanding influence in Pacific Island countries.
The linkage suggests Tokyo increasingly views maritime Southeast Asia and the Pacific Islands as a connected strategic space rather than separate diplomatic tracks. This approach also reflects Abe Shinzo’s vision of Japan as a “dot connector” linking like-minded partners across the Indo-Pacific. The Quad reinforced the same approach in Manila by pledging deeper cooperation with ASEAN on maritime security, critical technologies, economic security, and humanitarian assistance.
Most Southeast Asian governments, for their part, are seeking stronger maritime capabilities and more strategic options without wanting to be forced to choose between Beijing and either Washington or Tokyo.
China nevertheless views Japan’s expanding regional role with growing suspicion. Chinese officials warned against a “revival of militarism,” while Beijing rejected Motegi’s account of a brief exchange with Foreign Minister Wang Yi and state media dismissed the episode as political theater. More fundamentally, Chinese commentators increasingly portray Japan’s higher defense spending, long-range missile programs, deeper integration with the United States, and expanding security partnerships in Southeast Asia as evidence that Tokyo is abandoning its postwar restraint.
ASEAN governments are unlikely to respond uniformly. The Philippines and Vietnam have proven the most receptive to cooperation with Japan because of growing maritime pressure from China. Indonesia and Malaysia welcome capacity-building while remaining cautious about appearing aligned against Beijing. Cambodia and Laos remain more constrained by their close ties with China.
Yet even if the progress is uneven with individual partner countries, overall Japan is steadily institutionalizing security cooperation across Southeast Asia while linking it to a wider Indo-Pacific network extending to the Pacific Islands.
Whether that strategy succeeds will depend less on Beijing’s criticism than on whether Southeast Asian governments continue to see Tokyo as a partner that enhances their autonomy rather than constrains it.

articles.title: Tokayev Urges Russia to ‘Freeze’ Ukraine Conflict While Embracing ‘Allied Relationship’
articles.full_text:
Tokayev’s call for peace talks came alongside remarks on Kazakhstan’s enduring strategic cooperation and alliance with Russia.
Days after Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev publicly suggested to Russian President Vladimir Putin that he freeze the conflict with Ukraine and return to the negotiating table, Putin signed a pair of executive orders paving the way to begin talks with Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan to update their existing military-technical cooperation agreements.
These two events are not necessarily connected, but viewed together they serve to highlight the multidimensional relationships between the Central Asian states and Russia.
Tokayev met Putin in the Siberian city of Omsk for the Russia-Kazakhstan Forum of Interregional Cooperation on July 24-25. Speaking alongside Putin at the forum, Tokayev urged his Russian counterpart to return to the negotiating table.
“Perhaps it’s time to put this conflict on hold and return to the Istanbul 2.0 formula, since significant results have been achieved there,” Tokayev said, referring to talks hosted in the Turkish capital in March 2022 – shortly after Russia’s full-scale invasion began – and again in May 2025. 
That first round of talks in Istanbul in 2022, as Samuel Charap and Sergey Radchenko wrote in a 2024 article for Foreign Affairs, could have ended the war – but didn’t.
In other conflicts, such as Syria circa 2017, Kazakhstan has offered itself up as a mediator or a neutral venue.  
On July 25, Tokayev rejected that prospect, stating plainly, “I refuse to be a mediator, because I know that Russia is a great country, the Russian people are a great people, and, as they say, they can manage on their own without intermediaries.”
Nevertheless, Tokayev said he decided to “express my humble opinion today because people know about our meeting, they know I’m supposed to be in Omsk, and they asked me to convey this.” Tokayev acknowledged that Russia and Ukraine hold different positions, but said that there was an opportunity “to put this whole matter on hold.”
“All of this must be stopped,” Tokayev said of the conflict. “[W]hat’s happening, in my firm opinion, plays into the hands and delights of the adversaries of both Russia and Ukraine.”
Tokayev walked a diplomatic tightrope, reiterating Kazakhstan’s close ties and alliance with Russia while also pushing for peace.
“Have no doubt, we have always considered and continue to consider Russia a great nation. We are committed to strategic cooperation with Russia and to an allied relationship, no matter how difficult it may be,” he said, before adding, “We have always treated the Ukrainian people with respect.”
“The nature of this conflict is not entirely clear to many, including us,” Tokayev said before complimenting Putin’s flexibility in Alaska – where he met with U.S. President Donald Trump in August 2025. What was agreed to in Alaska is, ironically, also unclear. Last month, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that Russia and the United States did not reach any agreement in Alaska. Russian officials, however, continue to reference such agreements as a demonstration of Moscow’s ultimately potemkin willingness to pursue peace via negotiation.
In response to Tokayev’s comments, Putin reportedly replied that he would “inform Tokayev about the progress of affairs in the Ukrainian direction.”
Whether Tokayev’s nudge will yield productive talks is unclear. As reported by the Kyiv Independent, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov responded fairly negatively to Tokayev’s comments. He said “a freeze as such is impossible.”
“For us, there is a key condition: we must achieve our goals,” Peskov added.
Soon after Tokayaev’s comments, The Insider reported that two executive orders had been published via Moscow’s official legal information portal authorizing the Russian government to pursue negotiations with Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan over their existing military-technical cooperation agreements: a December 24, 2013 agreement with Kazakhstan (ratified in 2015) and a November 29, 2016 treaty with Uzbekistan.
The existing treaties govern not only the sale of Russian weapons to these countries but also mutual deliveries of defense products, including weapons and military vehicles, military-technical information, technologies, intellectual property, services, design, engineering, and technological operational documentation. The agreements provide for the repair and modernization of armaments, joint research and development, the establishment of joint manufacturing facilities, and human capacity building.
It’s not clear from the orders what precisely Russia wants to renegotiate. In its report, TASS – the state-owned Russian news agency – simply noted that neither agreement has been updated since they were signed. The orders are a single paragraph each and serve to simply authorize negotiations on amending the relevant agreements. 
The Ukraine war is most certainly the backdrop. Western sanctions have complicated exports between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, and Russia – in both directions. The European Union and the United States have banned the export of weapons and dual-use goods to Russia, which range from microchips to engines and drone parts. The militaries of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan primarily use Russian platforms, generating a line of potential leverage or at least shortage. In a recent report on Uzbekistan’s military, the Oxus Society for Central Asian Affairs noted, “The Uzbek Ground Forces possess one of the largest stockpiles of Russian and Soviet military equipment outside of Russia…” Uzbekistan, the same report said, does not “produce enough ammunition and supplies to meet its basic peacetime requirements and remains largely reliant on nations like Russia to keep its forces operational.”
In the tangled web of relations between the Central Asian states and Russia, Ukraine produces a kind of rorschach test: the perspective of the viewer, their biases and position, influences how they view a chain of events or interpret certain statements. Tokayev’s push for peace in Ukraine sits somewhat uncomfortably alongside Kazakhstan’s strategic alliance with Russia. How amending their military-technical agreement progresses will add more ink to the picture, but may not clarify the image.

articles.title: How Indonesia and Singapore Handle Information Pressure
articles.full_text:
From election debates to AI‑manipulated content, audiences in both countries rely on legacy media for credibility while increasingly consuming politics through fast, visual, and creator‑driven formats.
Trust in news continues to slide globally, yet when elections arrive, audiences in Indonesia and Singapore behave differently. New evidence from both countries shows that even in a fragmented, creator‑driven information ecosystem, voters still return to legacy media for credibility and reassurance.
The latest Reuters Institute Digital News Report highlighted a familiar trend: social media and video platforms have on average across markets overtaken news websites and apps, and global trust in news has fallen to 37 percent, the lowest level since 2015. A Eurobarometer survey across 27 EU states similarly found that two in three users seek political information on social media, and more than one-third follow influencers.
These patterns raise a critical question: do people rely on different information sources when the stakes are high? Studies conducted during the 2024 Indonesian presidential election and the 2025 Singapore general election suggest they do.
In Indonesia, a nationally representative two‑wave panel survey found that television remained the most accessed source of election news, followed by WhatsApp and face‑to‑face conversations. YouTube, TikTok, Facebook, and Instagram have grown rapidly, but they have not displaced TV’s central role. Print media has nearly vanished, with almost nine in ten respondents saying they never accessed it.
Trust patterns mirror usage. Indonesians placed the greatest trust in television and interpersonal conversations – not social media. During high‑stakes moments, voters seek not only speed but facts, familiarity, and accountability.
Singapore shows a similar pattern despite its more digitally saturated environment. During the 2025 general election, digital versions of legacy outlets such as CNA, The Straits Times, and Lianhe Zaobao were among the most used and trusted sources. Television remained the second most trusted medium across demographics. Print continues to decline, but the institutions behind it retain influence through digital migration.
Across both countries, the evidence is clear: legacy media has not disappeared; it has moved online. When voters need clarity, they turn to brands associated with editorial credibility.
Legacy media now competes in a transformed attention economy. Short‑form video, creator commentary, and podcasts have become central to political communication, especially among younger voters.
In Indonesia, voters aged 15-24 consumed election content primarily through TikTok, WhatsApp, TV, Instagram, and YouTube. Podcasts and influencers were key sources of political commentary. Singapore’s voters showed similar behavior: TikTok and YouTube were major platforms for younger voters, and nearly one‑third of all voters consumed podcasts daily during election time.
This shift has consequences. A policy proposal becomes a slogan; a debate becomes a few viral seconds; a candidate is remembered for a meme rather than a platform. Indonesia’s election survey captured this dynamic: around half watched the presidential debates in full, but 60 percent watched only post‑debate clips, which significantly shaped perceptions of candidates.
Short‑form content is not inherently harmful, but its emphasis on emotion and speed often comes at the expense of nuance. As politics becomes “snackable,” societies must ask how to preserve meaningful civic discussion. Digital literacy efforts must therefore expand beyond spotting fake news. Civic and political literacy – understanding how policies affect daily life, how governance works, and how framing shapes meaning – is increasingly essential.
AI‑generated content is adding new layers to election communication. In Indonesia, AI was used to create satire, engagement‑driven content and the viral “Gemoy” cartoons linked to the Prabowo‑Gibran campaign. These materials were not outright disinformation but subtle propaganda that is harder to regulate.
Exposure to deepfakes was limited, but belief in them followed partisan lines. Young and educated voters reported the highest exposure to misinformation – and the highest awareness of it.
Singapore’s electorate showed caution toward digitally manipulated content. About one‑third “sometimes” or “very often” encountered AI‑manipulated material, though most rarely did. Concern about AI misuse remained high across age and education groups.
The two countries diverge sharply on regulation. Singapore has adopted a proactive stance, passing the Elections (Integrity of Online Advertising) (Amendment) Act in 2024 to counter digitally manipulated content.
Indonesia, by contrast, faces legal gaps. Nearly half of Indonesian respondents were unaware of video‑editing software, making them more vulnerable to manipulation. Indonesia’s Electronic Information and Transactions Law and Election Law do not regulate generative AI use in elections. A court ruling in January 2025 – after the election – prohibited excessive alteration of candidate images.
Regulation alone cannot solve information manipulation, but it clarifies accountability and deters abuse. As technology accelerates, anticipatory regulatory frameworks – not just ex‑post measures – are increasingly necessary.
In an environment defined by fragmentation, speed, and manipulation, the challenge is not to resist change but to adapt without losing depth and accuracy. The lesson from Indonesia and Singapore is clear: when democracy is at stake, audiences still turn to credible institutions.
Sustaining that trust requires adaptable journalism, deeper civic literacy, and smarter regulation – so that voters can navigate high‑stakes moments with clarity rather than confusion.

articles.title: Alleged Cambodia Scam Kingpin Chen Zhi Could Face the Death Penalty in China
articles.full_text:
Myanmar follows Beijing’s lead in amending anti-scam laws as crime syndicates shift operations.
Chen Zhi, the chairman of Prince Holding Group, as seen in a publicity photo on the conglomerate’s website.
China knows how to send a stern message and the word out of Beijing this week will reverberate across the region, particularly in Myanmar, Cambodia, and Laos. Chen Zhi, the founder and chairman of Cambodia’s Prince Group and alleged mastermind of the country’s scam compound industry, just might be executed.
Authorities have beefed-up Chen’s charge sheet since his deportation in January from Cambodia to China, where he is facing prosecution – adding intentionally inflicting bodily injury.
If that causes death or severe injury especially through cruel means then under Chinese criminal law, it is punishable by a minimum jail term of 10 years and – ultimately – the death penalty.
The 38-year-old was also charged with copyright infringement and a previous count of concealing criminal proceeds was dropped, Chinese business magazine Caixin reported. That obviously pales against a possible death sentence, a penalty this journalist is opposed to, but Beijing has well flagged the risks.
On January 29, Xinhua announced that China had executed 11 members of the “Ming family criminal group” for crimes that included “intentional homicide, intentional injury, unlawful detention, fraud and [running a] casino establishment” through scam compounds in territories along the China-Myanmar border.
In Naypyidaw, the Myanmar military junta’s civil administration has followed suit and just approved amendments to its Anti-Online Scam Bill that confirms 10 years to life for the running of scam compounds and human trafficking networks, Agence France-Press reported.
The agency also confirmed that the death sentence can be administered for “violence, torture, unlawful arrest and detention, or cruel treatment against another person for the purpose of forcing them to commit online scams.”
Myanmar became synonymous with scam compounds after Chinese crime syndicates expanded their operations out of Cambodia and along Myanmar’s eastern border with Thailand, where small cities emerged around casino hubs in places like Shwe Kokko.
But word from the border has been consistent ever since early last year, when Thailand, with Chinese backing, launched a crackdown on the syndicates operating along its borders inside Myanmar, Cambodia, and Laos.
Sources in Mae Sot on the Thai side of the border say organized crime groups, in league with militias aligned with the military in Myanmar, have cut and run inland and further south and are now re-establishing themselves in much smaller units, staffed by willingly, tech-savvy people.
“The civil war has ground into stalemate and there are elements aligned with the military who are getting involved with Chinese organized crime and running scams to make money,” a source with the opposition People’s Defense Force said.
“I just spent a few days at Three Pagodas Pass and scam centers were everywhere,” she said. “I just got back. It took 20-hours to reach Mae Sot.
“Scammers have set-up operations inside small hotels and apartments and there’s a lot of them… there’s no one big identifiable compound but they are easy to spot. There is a war going on and they just look so out of place. It’s not like Shwe Kokko,” she added. “But new buildings are going up.”
Three Pagodas Pass sits in the Tenasserim Hills on the border between Thailand and Myanmar and is controlled by the Democratic Karen Benevolent Army (DKBA), which is aligned with the ruling junta but has rejected speculation of any involvement with the scam compounds.
They sit just inside the Myanmar border, and whoever controls the pass holds the advantage of the military high ground. The source added, “The DKBA is in charge and yes they are the controlling influence over scammers and what they’re doing now.”
With the collapse of Prince Bank and the seizure of almost $15 billion in assets by United States authorities, Chen remains the highest profile catch of this whole sorry saga.
Others have followed, including Li Xiong, former chairman of Huione Group, a Prince subsidiary, Hu Shi, apparently second to Chen at Prince, who has been arrested for falsifying documents, and Jinbei Group founder Liu Ren was also extradited from Cambodia.
China knows how to send a stern message and the word out of Beijing this week will reverberate across the region, particularly in Myanmar, Cambodia, and Laos. Authorities have beefed-up Chen’s charge sheet since his deportation in January from Cambodia to China, where he is facing prosecution – adding intentionally inflicting bodily injury.
If that causes death or severe injury especially through cruel means then under Chinese criminal law, it is punishable by a minimum jail term of 10 years and – ultimately – the death penalty.
The 38-year-old was also charged with copyright infringement and a previous count of concealing criminal proceeds was dropped, Chinese business magazine Caixin reported. That obviously pales against a possible death sentence, a penalty this journalist is opposed to, but Beijing has well flagged the risks.
On January 29, Xinhua announced that China had executed 11 members of the “Ming family criminal group” for crimes that included “intentional homicide, intentional injury, unlawful detention, fraud and [running a] casino establishment” through scam compounds in territories along the China-Myanmar border.
In Naypyidaw, the Myanmar military junta’s civil administration has followed suit and just approved amendments to its Anti-Online Scam Bill that confirms 10 years to life for the running of scam compounds and human trafficking networks, Agence France-Press reported.

articles.title: Following Expansion in China, Regional Private Equity Faces New Scrutiny in Southeast Asia
articles.full_text:
The Southeast Asian region is experiencing an unprecedented economic and industrial boom as a result of rising consumer demand, government decarbonization mandates as well as diversification priorities under the so-called “China Plus One” shift. The rapid expansion of electric vehicle (EV) adoption, battery manufacturing, logistics and consumer services is attracting a growing number of investors to growth opportunities across the member states of ASEAN.
The automotive and two-wheeler EV sector in Thailand, Indonesia’s battery cathode precursor manufacturing, Vietnam’s lithium-ion cell assembly, and the regionally booming sectors of third-party logistics (3PL) and digital consumer services have seen an uptick in investment from private equity firms originating in South Korea and Japan, as well as Greater China and Singapore. Many of these firms from different Asian financial centers first gained experience in China’s domestic market before opening up to the wider region.
Private equity firms have accumulated 10-20 years of investment experience in China on average before opening to Southeast Asia. This has posed both challenges and advantages. As recent geopolitical developments demonstrated – including lockdowns during the global pandemic, trade wars and the weaponization of supply chains – an overreliance on China can, in and of itself, represent a business risk. This is one reason companies are looking to diversify their manufacturing and supply chains as part of the China Plus One strategy by approaching alternative hubs in Vietnam, India, and Malaysia and beyond the region.
On the other hand, the extended timeline of their operations in China has granted these firms several advantages, including the opportunity to mature in a large domestic market and oversee several business cycles complete with contractions and expansions, as well as regulatory changes under the unique system of state capitalism.
South Korea’s MBK Partners provides one example of why this trajectory may merit closer scrutiny. Its China portfolio includes transactions involving state-linked automotive groups. The firm completed its acquisition of CAR Inc after negotiations with Beijing Automotive Group, a Beijing municipal state-owned enterprise. The transaction illustrates the extent to which some regional private equity activity in China has intersected with state-controlled industrial networks. MBK also co-invested in eHi Car Services – China’s second-largest car rental company – alongside Dongfeng Asset Management, associated with the state-owned Dongfeng Motor group, as part of a deal worth nearly a billion dollars.
Similar tension was also apparent in the United States, where at a reception held in Nashville in July, MBK Partners and Young Poong Group reportedly presented themselves to Tennessee stakeholders as the largest shareholder group supporting Project Crucible, a joint venture in Tennessee between KoreaZinc and the U.S. Department of War. KoreaZinc is a South Korean non-ferrous metal smelter and a strategic supplier of critical minerals to both the United States.
The event hosted by MBK-Young Poong coalition raises eyebrows because they previously opposed the US-backed initiative, highlighting in company communiqués that the project would place core national technology in the hands of the U.S. government. The event’s invitation indicated that Tennessee Governor Bill Lee was expected to attend, although he ultimate did not. This can be, in part, attributed to the fact that MBK and Young Poong have been engaged in a control battle against the current controlling shareholders of KoreaZinc and its current management since 2024. The episode has raised questions regarding MBK’s efforts to position itself publicly as a leading supporter of the JV developed by KoreaZinc, despite noted previous opposition to the initiative. Such cases underscore the need to examine how China-based relationships may shape private section expansion elsewhere across the West.
This mirrors the business strategies of several other Asian investors. Hong Kong-based BPEA EQT has spent billions in Greater China over the past three decades in sectors including healthcare, technology and logistics. The firm invested over $100 million in China’s MediTech Limited and raised over $1.2 billion to develop logistics properties in gateway cities across the country.
Japan’s Advantage Partners expanded into China in several sectors simultaneously, including in manufacturing, consumer and business services. Its investment in Qin Jia Yuan, a multimedia and advertising development company, represented a significant strategic growth opportunity.
Experience in these sectors become increasingly relevant as Southeast Asia’s current stage of development often resembles earlier stages of China’s growth.
Foreign direct investment is reaching record highs in the region, making it one of the fastest-growing outsourced logistics markets in the world, projected to reach over $216 billion in value. Malaysia and Singapore play significant roles in this. The region is also becoming a leader in the EV sector, and, importantly, this applies to both the adoption and the manufacturing of electric vehicles. Market penetration in new vehicle sales has recently surpassed 40 percent in countries like Vietnam and Singapore, while Indonesia secured deals surpassing a billion dollars in value from both BYD and Hyundai for the building of manufacturing plants.
MBK Partners’ experience managing mobility platforms in China includes transactions involving entities connected to major Chinese state-owned automotive groups. As it expands into Southeast Asia, those ties may invite closer examination from investors and regulators concerned with governance, strategic dependency and exposure to China-linked state interests. Hong Kong’s PAG and BPEA EQT, in addition to China’s own Hillhouse Investment, can adapt and expand their existing portfolio in logistics, manufacturing and consumer businesses. Similarly, Japan’s Advantage Partners can help scale Southeast Asian businesses in areas ranging from consumer packaging to pharmaceuticals. More broadly, for regional investors with extensive operating histories in China, this experience is therefore not merely a commercial exercise. Prior partnerships with Chinese state-owned groups require closer scrutiny as firms enter new Southeast Asian markets, particularly where investments touch strategic infrastructure, mobility or critical supply chains.
Strategic corporate investors are already signaling which sectors private equity firms might follow them into in the near future. Industrial giants such as battery and EV firms CATL, BYD, Gotion High-Tech and EVE Energy are transforming Southeast Asia into a fully integrated production area. They are capitalizing on Indonesia’s vast nickel reserves in upstream investments, the push for EVs implemented by Thailand’s government, and the scaling up of existing operations in Malaysia and Vietnam.
Regional private equity firms are positioned to contribute much more to Southeast Asia’s growth than private capital alone. Investors from South Korea, Hong Kong, Japan and mainland China bring several years of sector-specific operational expertise to develop the EV, manufacturing, logistics and consumer services industries.

articles.title: Indonesia Eyes Closer Relations With Madagascar
articles.full_text:
A recent bilateral exchange hinted that Jakarta is taking a greater interest in its Austronesian cousin on the other side of the Indian Ocean.
Madagascar’s Foreign Minister Alice N’Diaye shakes hands with Indonesian Foreign Minister Sugiono during here visit to Jakarta, Indonesia, June 3, 2026.
Last month, Madagascar’s Foreign Minister Alice N’Diaye made an official working visit to Indonesia, her first trip to the country.
During her visit, the two nations announced the establishment of a Joint Commission for Bilateral Cooperation which aims to deepen and drive their strategic and economic partnership. They also announced the granting of mutual visa exemptions for service and diplomatic passport holders.
Following his meeting with N’Diaye, Indonesian Foreign Minister Sugiono called for the two nations to strengthen their economic ties and remove travel barriers.
“Madagascar has a very strategic geographical position, which also serves as a gateway to Africa,” he stated, as per Indonesian news agency Antara, noting that “they possess natural resources, especially minerals needed for industry and advanced technology.”
The two ministers further pledged to broaden bilateral economic and trade cooperation in the areas of the blue economy, agriculture, renewable energy, fisheries and tourism.
Madagascar also announced its intention to open its first diplomatic mission in Indonesia, which would also be its first in Southeast Asia, although no specific timeframe has been given. During the meeting, Sugiono expressed optimism that the embassy opening could give Madagascar the means to engage more closely with ASEAN member states. N’Diaye described Indonesia as a crucial partner in “anchoring Madagascar to wider international economic dynamics.”
Indonesia surprisingly has a lot in common with Madagascar, the largest island in both Africa and the Indian Ocean. Both nations are full members of the Indian Ocean Rim Association and Non-Aligned Movement (NAM). The two countries also share a common Austronesian identity. Madagascar was first settled during or before the mid-first millennium by Austronesian peoples, who sailed across the Indian Ocean from what is today the Indonesian archipelago. Today, the Malagasy peoples, an Austronesian-speaking ethnic group, make up the overwhelming majority of Madagascar’s population and speak a language with a common ancestry to modern Indonesian.
Despite the ethnolinguistic links between the two countries, however, contemporary bilateral relations until now have been very much underdeveloped.
Nonetheless, N’Diaye’s recent visit to Jakarta demonstrates the potential benefits for Indonesia of strengthening its bilateral strategic and economic ties with its distant African cousin.
Traditionally, Indonesia’s principal geostrategic focus has been its natural leadership of ASEAN. But Jakarta is also an Indian Ocean nation and has a strong legacy of leadership in the Global South. Indonesia hosted the historic 1955 Asian African conference in Bandung, which subsequently laid the foundations for the formation of the NAM in the early 1960s. President Prabowo Subianto has said that during his presidency, “there will be a special focus on Africa.”
Indeed, Madagascar could become an increasingly important partner for Indonesia in the years to come. Major shipping corridors like the Mozambique Channel and Cape Sainte Marie are located close to Madagascar, connecting Africa and Asia. The ongoing Red Sea crisis and Iran war has forced many ships to reroute around Africa’s southern tip through sea lanes near Madagascar. Therefore, the security of the maritime trade routes near Madagascar could become an issue of increasing interest for Jakarta.
There are also good reasons for Indonesia to deepen its defense ties with Madagascar, particularly in maritime security cooperation. Indonesia could help increase the small Madagascar navy’s at sea security capabilities by running regular bilateral maritime patrols, holding annual joint military exercises, and port visits. This could empower both nations to address shared border security threats including illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing, transnational crime, and piracy.
In 2022, then Madagascar Defense Minister Richard Rakotonirina met with Luhut Binsar Pandjaitan, Indonesia’s then coordinating minister of maritime and investment affairs in Bali. During the meeting, Rakotonirina said that Indonesia’s leadership was “important in maintaining the security of the maritime area in the Indo-Pacific, especially in the Indian Ocean.” Luhut explained that Indonesia was committed to “protect the Indian Ocean as a joint strategic area,” although did not explain how this would work in practice.
Madagascar is a hotspot for IUU fishing, and the country is struggling to curb illegal fishing vessels from entering its waters and exclusive economic zone. The country is currently losing an estimated $80 million a year from IUU fishing, which is also threatening the livelihoods of an estimated 1,250 fishing communities along Madagascar’s coasts.
Earlier this year, as part of its naval diplomacy efforts in Africa, the Indonesian Navy’s new frigate KRI Prabu Siliwangi made port visits to Nigeria, South Africa, and Mauritius. Marcellus Hakeng Jayawibawa, an analyst at the National Resilience Institute of Indonesia said that the visits were a clear indication that the Indonesian Navy was transforming from a “traditionally defensive maritime force to an actor capable of power projection.”
The Madagascar and Indonesian militaries could also ensure both have reciprocal access to their respective military training areas. The training would be particularly beneficial for Madagascar’s defense forces, especially those stationed along the coastal and maritime areas of their country. Indonesia could provide Madagascar defense cadets with greater access to military education programs in Indonesia, building on limited past initiatives. (Rakotonirina is fluent in Bahasa Indonesia and is a graduate of the Indonesian military academy.)
On an economic and multilateral level, Indonesia could bring Madagascar closer to ASEAN. It can do this by advocating for Madagascar to become a dialogue partner of the 11-nation bloc, and joining the list of nations that participate in ASEAN-led mechanisms, including the ASEAN Regional Forum and the East Asia Summit.
Indonesia is set to reach new heights of economic growth and confidence in the coming years. It is predicted to become the fourth-largest economy in the world by 2050. This will likely make it a more active player in the Indian Ocean and Africa. Ultimately, through a more substantial relationship with Madagascar, its distant relation, Indonesia could begin to exert some of its growing economic and military clout in Africa and the Indian Ocean.

articles.title: The Quad and ASEAN’s First Step Off The Fence
articles.full_text:
For the first time, the Quad issued a dedicated joint statement on cooperation with ASEAN.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio meets with Indo-Pacific Quad Foreign Ministers in Manila, Philippines, July 22, 2026.
The East Asia Summit, a forum for strategic, political, and economic dialogue comprising 19 countries, convened its 16th Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in Manila on July 23. The summit, however, assumed significance because of events that occurred on its sidelines.
To begin with, the Quad Foreign Ministers met again and reiterated their commitments unveiled at the 11th Quad Foreign Ministers’ Meeting in Delhi two months ago. But it wasn’t their mere gathering that caught attention.
For the first time, the Quad issued a dedicated joint statement on cooperation with ASEAN, rather than just meeting alongside the regional grouping. The ministers framed themselves as “ASEAN Comprehensive Strategic Partners” and tied their agenda to “the practical implementation of the ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-Pacific.” The statement identified four broad areas of cooperation: “maritime and transnational security, economic prosperity and security, critical and emerging technologies, and humanitarian assistance and emergency response.”
Reconvening in the same city where the Quad was revived in 2017, this time to issue a joint statement directly highlighting cooperation with ASEAN, is a response to critics who question the Quad’s lack of engagement with regional countries.
The fact that this joint statement, even though quite vague, came at ASEAN’s premier politico-security forum, of which China is also a founding member, is suggestive of two things.
On the one hand, it reflected the Quad’s willingness to overcome its appeasement of China. So far, despite being inherently a counterweight to China, the Quad has often resisted steps that can be seen as enraging Beijing. The meeting in Manila amounts to the shedding of that longstanding hesitation. For the Quad to hold its huddle there, in what is often described as China’s own strategic neighborhood, is a pointed signal aimed at Beijing.
On the other hand, the fact that ASEAN accepted and enabled the Quad’s effort to insert itself as a stakeholder with a collective interest in the region is significant. Beijing has repeatedly described the Quad as an Asian NATO and has made its discomfort with the grouping known. Further, ASEAN has always sought to avoid becoming an arena for great power rivalry. Beijing is a full participant in the East Asia Summit and the ASEAN Regional Forum. 
Thus, the signal emerging from ASEAN is just as important, and arguably braver. The bloc communicated to Beijing that it is not afraid to engage the Quad, and that it might like to do more of that. The visible loosening of ASEAN’s reflex to keep the Quad at arm’s length will not be lost on Beijing.
So, what now? It is worth recalling that the foreign ministers’ meetings of both the EAS and the Quad at Manila came days after a violent clash between Chinese and Filipino forces near the disputed Second Thomas Shoal.
However, the Quad refrained from collectively condemning China’s actions. Japan was the only Quad country to call out China. It raises an uncomfortable question. If the grouping believes in “ASEAN Centrality” as the guiding principle of its Indo-Pacific policy, it cannot avoid commenting on China’s unilateral actions against the ASEAN member countries. 
The formulation that the Quad is “not an anti-China grouping” has been useful because of its ambiguity. But as cooperation deepens, both the Quad and ASEAN will confront a genuine dilemma over whether to explicitly name China and its actions. 
If the two sides want a proof of concept that sidesteps the more politically difficult questions, disaster response and maritime domain awareness are natural areas to begin with, given that a baseline level of cooperation already exists. After Typhoon Yagi struck Vietnam in 2024, the Quad pledged over $4 million in relief efforts, and after the 2025 Myanmar earthquake, it committed more than $30 million towards humanitarian assistance. Building on these precedents, the Quad and ASEAN could establish a regional rapid-response protocol covering coordination, logistics and emergency communications.
A similar approach could be adopted in the maritime domain. Through the Indo-Pacific Partnership for Maritime Domain Awareness (IPMDA), launched in 2022, the Quad provides maritime tracking data to some ASEAN states. This could be expanded into a more formal arrangement for regular information-sharing across the bloc.
ASEAN has opened the door to a more substantive relationship with the Quad, and that achievement should not be underestimated. Given that the group has spent much of the past year fielding questions about drift and division, the fact of another meeting itself has value.

Thus, the signal emerging from ASEAN is just as important, and arguably braver. The bloc communicated to Beijing that it is not afraid to engage the Quad, and that it might like to do more of that. The visible loosening of ASEAN’s reflex to keep the Quad at arm’s length will not be lost on Beijing.
So, what now? It is worth recalling that the foreign ministers’ meetings of both the EAS and the Quad at Manila came days after a violent clash between Chinese and Filipino forces near the disputed Second Thomas Shoal.
However, the Quad refrained from collectively condemning China’s actions. Japan was the only Quad country to call out China. It raises an uncomfortable question. If the grouping believes in “ASEAN Centrality” as the guiding principle of its Indo-Pacific policy, it cannot avoid commenting on China’s unilateral actions against the ASEAN member countries. 
The formulation that the Quad is “not an anti-China grouping” has been useful because of its ambiguity. But as cooperation deepens, both the Quad and ASEAN will confront a genuine dilemma over whether to explicitly name China and its actions. 
If the two sides want a proof of concept that sidesteps the more politically difficult questions, disaster response and maritime domain awareness are natural areas to begin with, given that a baseline level of cooperation already exists. After Typhoon Yagi struck Vietnam in 2024, the Quad pledged over $4 million in relief efforts, and after the 2025 Myanmar earthquake, it committed more than $30 million towards humanitarian assistance. Building on these precedents, the Quad and ASEAN could establish a regional rapid-response protocol covering coordination, logistics and emergency communications.
A similar approach could be adopted in the maritime domain. Through the Indo-Pacific Partnership for Maritime Domain Awareness (IPMDA), launched in 2022, the Quad provides maritime tracking data to some ASEAN states. This could be expanded into a more formal arrangement for regular information-sharing across the bloc.
ASEAN has opened the door to a more substantive relationship with the Quad, and that achievement should not be underestimated. Given that the group has spent much of the past year fielding questions about drift and division, the fact of another meeting itself has value.
articles.summary: For the first time, the Quad issued a dedicated joint statement on cooperation with ASEAN.

articles.title: A New – and Old – China Human Rights Agenda at the United Nations
articles.full_text:
Why did China support the re-election of Volker Turk as U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights?
Volker Türk, United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, addresses the informal meeting of the General Assembly plenary to hear a briefing on missing persons, Apr. 2, 2025.
Volker Turk, the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, has won re-election to hold that post for another four years. Several governments objected to the process; 144 others, including China, voted in support of a second term for him.
Over the past four years Chinese authorities have deepened repression. The Chinese government inflicts collective punishment on the families of defenders and prisoners of conscience and has a disturbing track record of defenders dying in detention. Its enthusiasm for transnational repression – an effort to silence critics of the Chinese government outside the country – is growing, and it increasingly thwarts human rights scrutiny by U.N. bodies. In fact, the Chinese government ranks high among the states targeting human rights defenders for engaging with U.N. human rights mechanisms. 
While Turk has offered up occasional critiques of Beijing’s human rights abuses, ranging from calling for abusive laws to be repealed and condemning the treatment of individual prisoners of conscience, his efforts have caused Beijing no real discomfort, and not kept pace with that regime’s violations.
Just weeks before Turk formally took up the role of High Commissioner in October 2022, the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) published a landmark report alleging that Chinese government policies toward Uyghurs and other Turkic communities entailed mass arbitrary detention, torture, and family separations. The report concluded that the Chinese government’s actions “may… constitute crimes against humanity.” 
Pressed by governments, journalists, and activists since then, Turk has said that there “is no crack of light” between him and the report’s findings. Yet over the past four years, he and his senior colleagues opted to pursue the diplomatic cul-de-sac of dialogues with those responsible for the abuses: Chinese government officials. He has rarely met with the victims and survivors of Beijing’s abuses.
Turk cannot now say that he needs time to cycle through the standard diplomatic playbook with Beijing – those efforts do not appear to have yielded results, allowing further human rights deteriorations to go unaddressed. If in his second term he wants to make meaningful progress toward redressing deepening repression inside China – and halting Chinese government abuses in other countries – he should prioritize four steps, all of them immediately achievable.
First, when the U.N. Human Rights Council – the world’s flagship political human rights body – goes into session in September, Turk should seize the opportunity to brief member states on what he has tried to achieve for victims and survivors since that September 2022 report. He should explain why those efforts have faltered, and, most importantly, what he plans to do instead, such as updating the findings of the report, and interviewing witnesses. Nothing prohibits him from taking such actions, and doing so would at least rob Chinese diplomats of the opportunity to brag – as they do in the halls of the Palais des Nations – about having shut down discussion about their grotesque abuses.
Second, Turk could reallocate a resource over which he has a great deal of control: time. He should spend as much time with the victims and survivors of Beijing’s abuses as he has spent with the perpetrators. Not only should he hear their horror stories, but he should be seen to have met with them. Beijing is known for threatening officials not to meet people or attend events representing ideas it does not like, often labeling them anti-China or “terrorists.” Too many governments take this threat seriously, and the result is to further disempower people with legitimate positions on human rights – particularly victims. 
Third, Turk should set out ambitious agendas to address alleged Chinese government crimes against humanity, including articulating legal pathways to accountability. But he should also directly address the concerns repeatedly set out by U.N. human rights experts, known as “special procedures,” who have for six years sounded alarms about Beijing’s non-compliance with and manipulation of its obligations under international human rights law. They have asked for the kind of help leadership requires: a special session at the HRC on China, the appointment of an expert specifically on China, greater attention to Beijing’s growing hostility toward U.N. human rights mechanisms.
Finally, Turk can help deny Beijing with “blue washing” its reputation through U.N. human rights reviews. Chinese diplomats shrilly insist there are no human rights abuses in the country. The best response to this position? Relentless public confrontation using facts and specifics: that allegations of crimes against humanity have also come from U.N. experts on arbitrary detention. That Beijing’s new “Ethnic Unity and Progress Law,” which is diametrically opposed to the government’s international obligations against discrimination, is another profound threat to the future of Tibetans, Uyghurs, and so many other groups already at risk of state-sponsored identity erasure. Nearly all 300 of the human rights lawyers detained, disbarred, or disappeared across China in 2015 have been unable to resume their essential – and legally protected – work. 
Turk has a unique opportunity – he knows the job, the institution, the geopolitics, and now has four full years to put that knowledge to good use. He is demonstrably comfortable challenging some permanent members of the U.N. Security Council, particularly Russia and the United States. His office has demonstrated its capacity to document Beijing’s human rights crimes; other U.N. human rights bodies regularly provide strong evidence of other abuses. He needs to understand the risks it takes for victims from China to reach out to his office, and how unique a responsibility he has speaking with them and on their behalf. 
The only outstanding question: will he put his new term to use in service of victims and survivors of Beijing’s abuses, and of accountability? That would be an outstanding legacy. Without such leadership the United Nations will become progressively less relevant on human rights – exactly the outcome several powerful states would like to see.

articles.title: Why Did China Sanction 2 High-Tech Institutions in Poland?
articles.full_text:
Beijing has offered no explanation for why these particular Polish entities were selected, but several recent developments are worth noting.
The main building of the Wrocław University of Science and Technology.
China has imposed sanctions on two Polish entities linked to the country’s defense and high-tech sectors. The move comes in response to the European Union’s 21st sanctions package against Russia. The latest EU measures targeted several companies from China and Hong Kong that are accused of supplying Moscow with technologies and components used in Russia’s war against Ukraine.
One of the Polish entities placed on China’s export control list is Wrocław University of Science and Technology (WUST), one of Poland’s leading technical universities with recognized expertise in satellite technologies, and space-related research. The other is Vigo Photonics, a high-tech manufacturer supplying components for the Polish Armed Forces as well as the Military University of Technology, Poland’s premier institution for military engineering.
This is not Beijing’s first move of this kind. In April, China’s Ministry of Commerce added seven European entities to its export control list in response to European measures targeting Chinese companies.
Responding to questions from the Polish Press Agency on July 27, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian emphasized that the decision was “a response to the EU’s erroneous move of listing and sanctioning Chinese companies” and stressed that “the measures do not target any specific country.”
Beijing’s decision to sanction WUST is particularly striking. The university participates in EU-funded projects on military drones and battlefield artificial intelligence. At the same time, it has been engaged in joint semiconductor research with Chinese universities.
“Wrocław University of Science and Technology is a poli-technical school with tradition and impact for regional and domestic Polish industry,” Krzysztof Karwowski, a researcher at the SGH Warsaw School of Economics, told The Diplomat.
“It is a leader primarily in advanced photonics and is the longest-established research center in this field in Poland, creates a number of engineering partnerships in Europe, and is the core of the Polish space industry: microsatellites and satellite optics for security.”
As for the implications of China’s move, Karwowski said it was “difficult to assess” at this point – “we will know them in the coming weeks.” 
He pointed out that WUST and Shanghai Jiao Tong University sealed a “partnership in the field of design and research on semiconductors” last year. “Given China’s activity at Polish academia, WUST may re-prioritize its collaborations in Asia, of which it has a number, to universities in India, Japan, or Korea,” Karwowski predicted.
The university’s inclusion on the sanctions list is puzzling, given its close scientific cooperation with Chinese institutions.
The other sanctioned entity, Vigo Photonics, specializes in manufacturing infrared detectors, building on research developed in cooperation with institutions such as the Military University of Technology. The company’s products are used across the energy, medical, railway, and defense sectors.
For the Polish Armed Forces, Vigo supplies infrared detectors used in unmanned aerial vehicles, precision-guided munitions, and self-guided weapons. Its components are also integrated into observation and targeting systems installed on armored vehicles and air-defense systems acquired by the Polish military.
Interestingly, the company itself had anticipated the possibility of Chinese restrictions. According to Vigo’s public statement: 
Aware of this risk, the company has for several years sourced these substrates primarily from suppliers in Japan and Europe, capable of covering its full demand. The company also maintains inventory sufficient for more than one year of production, ensuring continuity in manufacturing infrared detectors and modules.
Importantly, inclusion on China’s export control list does not automatically prohibit all trade. Under Chinese regulations, entities such as Vigo Photonics and Wrocław University of Science and Technology may still receive dual-use goods from China, provided exporters obtain the appropriate government license. In practice, this means Beijing retains discretion over future deliveries rather than imposing an outright embargo.
Beijing has offered no explanation for why these particular Polish entities were selected. While it is tempting to construct a broader geopolitical narrative, several recent developments are worth noting.
First, WUST is located only around 20 kilometers from the site of the recently announced Polish-Taiwanese Foxconn investment. Just weeks ago, Polish and Taiwanese officials unveiled plans for Taiwan to help revive two major industrial projects in Poland: an electric vehicle factory originally expected to be developed with Chinese partners, and a semiconductor project left behind after Intel abandoned its investment near Wrocław.
Second, the sanctions coincide with Poland’s growing role in Europe’s space sector. Two weeks ago, the European Space Agency announced that a new ESA Center for Civil Security and Resilience will be established in Warsaw, supporting the development of European capabilities in strategically important fields. Space technologies remain one of the fastest-growing arenas of geopolitical competition between China and Western countries, and as Karwowski noted, WUST is central to Poland’s space program.
Third, Beijing may also be responding to Poland’s increasingly visible political engagement with Taiwan. Earlier this month, former Polish Prime Minister Beata Szydło led a delegation of Members of the European Parliament from the European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR) group to Taiwan, where they met President Lai Ching-te and senior representatives of Taiwan’s government and business community.
In crafting its latest sanctions, China may have chosen Polish institutions that are important enough to send a political message, but not so important that they would seriously damage scientific or business cooperation. In this sense, the sanctions appear to be more of a political signal than an attempt to cause major economic harm.

articles.title: The ‘Poisonous Heart’: Australia’s Most Secretive Base Draws New Scrutiny
articles.full_text:
The largest U.S. spy facility in the region attracted a massive protest action amid rising concerns about the Australia-U.S. alliance.
Protesters demand the closure of Pine Gap during a march to the base, July 20, 2026.
“In 1962, they took my grandfather, the Americans,” said Arrerente Elder Aunty Felicity while standing outside of Pine Gap, the largest U.S. spy base in Australia. 
She handed a printed letter to the Australian Federal Police Inspector Ken Napier at the gates of Pine Gap. 
Three generations of the Hayes family, the traditional owners of Kuyunba, stood next to the land occupied for 60 years by the largest Australia-U.S. joint defense facility in Australia.
Established in 1966, without the consent of traditional owners, the Pine Gap signals intelligence facility sits roughly 15 kilometers from Alice Springs. The access road leading to the base is lined with ominous signs warning, “NO THROUGH ROAD, GO BACK.” 
Percolated by the hum of drones overhead, the perimeter has all the markings of a spy base: high impenetrable gates marked by the strategic placement of surveillance apparatus. Access to sacred sites has been restricted for decades, hemmed in by Pine Gap’s edges. 
And on July 20, Aunty Felicity was joined by hundreds of activists to challenge the continued existence of the U.S. spy facility. Anti-militarist activists, academics and Traditional Owners traveled across the country, some from as far as 2,000km away, to reach the desert in the heart of Australia. It was the largest protest against Pine Gap since 1987, where some 300 people were arrested. 
AFP inspector Ken Napier greeted the Hayes family as they walked up to the gate to deliver the letter.  “Welcome,” he said.
Wyonna Hayes, the daughter of Aunty Felicity, looked angry as she responded, “You’re welcome to my country.”
Aunty Felicity delivered a speech, asking for the land, the Kuyunba, to be returned to the traditional owners. 
Many of Pine Gap’s custodians, including Aunty Felicity herself, live just a few kilometers away at Irrkerlantye, also known as White Gate, in conditions that stand in glaring contrast to the base’s heavily resourced compound.
The White Gate community lacks basic services that much of Australia takes for granted: water is trucked in, power comes from a small set of solar panels, and there is no sewerage. 
“We want people to support us to close down Pine Gap,” Aunty Felicity said, standing beside her sister Wyona, and daughter Jaquita. 
“We want them to know it’s a sacred site.” 
But she is also concerned about people she has never met. Among her requests is compensation for families in Gaza who have lost relatives in a war she said the base has helped enable. 
“We don’t want to be feeling guilty all the time,” she said, “when bad things are happening overseas to the little ones.”
“We’re not the ones controlling that facility,” she continued, “but we feel guilty that it’s coming from our land.” 
The police had set up two checkpoints before the march had even reached the base: one several kilometers out on the highway to check identification, and a second closer to the gate to stop the march on foot. 
The protesters were undeterred. Chanting and banging on drums they cried, “Close Pine Gap,” “Shut it down,” and “Always was, always will be Aboriginal land.”
Later that morning, a lone protester, Aahana Nag, locked herself to the steering wheel of a car blocking the base’s only access road, closing it for just over an hour before her arrest.
“The United States has displaced the custodians of these lands and has built an intelligence facility that provides critical intelligence for their illegal military operations,” Nag said afterwards. 
“This base is material proof of the federal government’s investment in U.S. wars that do not serve us.”
The action was the climax of a three-day convergence devoted to the history of U.S. militarism in the Northern Territory, organized by activist groups Mparntwe for Falastin and the Anti-Militarism Action Network. With over 600 in attendance, it focused on the history of Pine Gap and the resistance to it.
Convergence organizer Jorgen Doyle attributed the action’s success to a growing unease in Australia over the U.S. alliance. 
“It’s a really compelling geopolitical moment,” he said, “to contest Pine Gap and everything that it represents.” 
“Northern Australia is the top overseas location for US Air Force and Navy construction spending,” he added, referring to a report in Reuters published in 2024. According to the report, more than $300 million was set aside over several years under U.S. congressional defense authorizations to fund the construction. 
According to Dr. Richard Tanter, Pine Gap is as secretive as it is misunderstood. 
Widely considered Australia’s leading expert on Pine Gap, Tanter is a senior research associate at the Nautilus Institute for Security and Sustainability, where he has tracked the base’s expansion for over a decade, building on research alongside the late Des Ball and fellow researcher Bill Robinson. 
He told the convergence that the government’s habit of describing Pine Gap as a single facility is misleading.
articles.summary: The largest U.S. spy facility in the region attracted a massive protest action amid rising concerns about the Australia-U.S. alliance.

articles.title: Christianity in China: Testing Religious Freedom
articles.full_text:
The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Dr. Paul H. B. Chang – associate professor in the Department of Religious Studies at the University of California at Riverside and author of “The Spiritual Person: An Intellectual Biography of Watchman Nee” (Oxford 2026) – is the 519th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”
Identify the top three trends of Christianity in China.
I would say that probably the top three trends are the continued growth and vibrancy of Christianity in China, the increasing scrutiny and pressure placed on Christian organizations and their activities by the CCP [Chinese Community Party], and Chinese Christians’ theological and practical responses to their changing political and social environments. 
Although I use the word Christian, here and for the rest of the interview I am really speaking primarily of Protestants. In China, both legally and linguistically, Protestants and Catholics operate almost as two separate religions. Practically speaking, there is significant interaction and overlap but an expert on Chinese Catholicism would be better placed to talk about how much of this interview applies to Chinese Catholic circles. 
I also want to clarify that my work mostly centers on what one might consider more abstract, strictly theological trends. Thus, the top three trends I personally find most interesting relate to Chinese Christian perspectives on the nature and role of the church, differing doctrines on salvation, and contrasting perspectives on human nature. 
As far as the church is concerned, like all Christians, Chinese Christians have a longstanding interest in balancing the needs of the local and the universal church. They have thought a lot about how authority and administration can be both locally responsive and universally coherent. There is also a related, ongoing debate among Chinese Christians about how much the church should engage with secular society, both in terms of the government and in terms of wider cultural trends. 
Then, in terms of salvation, I think Chinese Christians once again have their own interesting, internal debate that roughly corresponds to theological trends outside of China. Whereas Reformed Christians have focused on more forensic, systematic perspectives on salvation, Watchman Nee is representative of an alternative train of thought that sees salvation as something more organic, seated in the union between the human and the divine.
This leads into my third perspective – that is, contrasting perspectives on human nature. Once again, I see the two main intellectual options as being something like a Reformed tradition, where the divine and human are more strictly delineated and kept apart, and a more mystical perspective, which sees some sort of ontological union as not only as possible but fundamental. 
Examine Western misconceptions about Chinese Christians.
Especially for Chinese Christians who follow or are influenced by Watchman Nee, their primary concern is not with political repression nor with asking for political support from outside China. Their theological mission is largely orthogonal to political changes and continues whether there is widespread support or disapprobation. And yet, they are very interested in communicating their universal vision with the world. 
They have a message for Western Christianity, indeed, for the Western secular world at large – namely that Jesus is coming and that sadly, most Christians and churches have not met his standard and may be found lacking on Jesus’s return. Few Westerners have heard their teaching that human beings should prepare for the end by being united in pure, local churches. In such local congregations, individual members can practice self-denial in self-sacrificing love for one another. This stands in stark contrast to this modern age of self-indulgence and self-promotion, which, they would argue, brings only misery.
Describe the scope of Watchman Nee’s faith and intellectual leadership beyond China.
Nee’s message is quite legible and even attractive to Westerners, especially to those of an evangelical Christian heritage. During the later years of his imprisonment, especially during the 1960s and 1970s, he became something of a cause célèbre among readers throughout the world, as a living example of a Christian suffering for his faith. He is quite readable in Chinese and he wrote a few key books in eloquent English as well, such as “The Normal Christian Life.” His writings have sold millions of copies and have been translated into dozens of languages. 
Furthermore, his influence shows no sign of slowing down, even more than 50 years after his death. In fact, given his popularity in non-Western Christian circles, such as in Africa and Latin America, it is quite possible that he has more readers than ever in 2026. 
All of this means that Watchman Nee belongs to a very select group of Chinese thinkers whose ideas and writings have spread beyond China and the Sinosphere and can truly be considered part of a global intellectual conversation. This small circle includes figures such as Confucius, Lao Zi, and Mao Zedong. Like them, Nee’s influence is not only broad but also deep. While many have casually read or appreciated Nee’s work, for some people, it has become a central moral compass and a guide to their human lives. In thousands of congregations on all six continents, there are hundreds of thousands of avid readers of Nee’s work who actively promote his perspectives on the Bible and on the ideal shape of Christian life. 
In these arenas, Nee’s clear message is that traditional or nominal Christianity alone cannot accomplish God’s goal and purpose for humanity. What God seeks is not adherents who donate money, defend orthodox doctrines, or perform certain rituals faithfully, but true worshippers whose entire lives come out of a radical root of self-denial. This self-denial is neither asceticism nor harsh self-treatment, but the spontaneous forgetting of the self that comes out of a deep love for Christ and the church. 
Explain the significance of recognition by the 111th (2009-2011) and 113th (2013-2015) U.S. Congress of Watchman Nee’s contributions to Christian thought in China.  
In both the 111th and 113th U.S. Congress, Watchman Nee was formally recognized by members of the United States Congress. These are more formal, political manifestations of the larger grassroots support Nee has generally received over the decades. In Christian circles, Nee has been lauded by influential figures across the Protestant spectrum ranging from Jerry Falwell and Carl Henry to Kenneth Hagin and Benny Hinn. Nee has even found followers in popular culture, including Bono and other members of the Irish rock band, U2, who seriously considered giving up their career in popular music because of Nee’s teachings on the self. 
All of these point to the rather undeniable facts that I believe are tacitly acknowledged even within Chinese government circles, namely that Watchman Nee, and his most significant follower Witness Lee, are important figures of world history. As the 113th U.S. Congress statement pointed out, it is ironic that with China’s growing presence on the global stage, some of its greatest thinkers cannot even be legally read within its own borders and their influence abroad cannot be openly acknowledged.
Assess the impact of Watchman Nee’s Christian thought on religious freedom in China-U.S. people-to-people relations.  
Nee’s relationship with religious freedom is interesting. He held to a core set of non-negotiable beliefs for which he was willing to suffering imprisonment and even martyrdom, like many Christians before him. Besides these core, rather theological values, he was willing to compromise and work with the government quite a lot. He felt that obedience to human authority as an extension of God’s authority was a key Christian virtue, and while he was imprisoned, he seems to have behaved himself as an exemplary inmate, except in his unwillingness to recant his faith. 
The people-to-people relationships between Nee’s followers within and outside of China are a key test case for the limits and possibilities for religious speech in civic and political spaces. Individual followers of Nee may and do hold a range of political opinions. Nevertheless, as a corporate body – that is, as the church – they are categorically opposed to direct involvement in politics, except to obey any explicit commands that do not contradict the gospel. It is hard to imagine a more politically quietist Protestant group. 
And yet, despite their quiescent nature, the very fact of their constituting a moral community does create an independent authority within the larger body politic. I suppose that from a completely paranoid perspective, even a completely subservient church may seem to pose a threat because of its independent existence. Still, members of congregations that follow Nee have struck me as model citizens wherever I have met them, whether in the U.S. or China. They tend to be scrupulously honest in their personal and professional lives and see a law-abiding, respectful attitude toward government as a meaningful part of their personal piety and Christian witness.
