articles.title: Malaysian Authorities Detain More Than 100 Rohingya Asylum Seekers Outside UNHCR Office
articles.full_text:
The detention of the group, who were reportedly driven out of a settlement in Penang on Sunday, comes amid rising public hostility toward Rohingya refugees.
Malaysian authorities yesterday detained more than 100 Rohingya Muslim asylum seekers who had ‌gathered outside the office of the United Nations refugee agency in Kuala Lumpur, after being evicted from their settlement in the northern state of Penang.
According to a report by the New Straits Times, the group was transferred in four police vehicles from outside the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) at around 8:20 p.m. yesterday, along with “luggage and personal belongings.”
The paper today quoted Kuala Lumpur police chief Fadil Marsus as saying that 113 refugees, including 110 Rohingya, were being held at police headquarters. Fadil also said checks conducted during the documentation process at the police headquarters found that all the Rohingya refugees possessed valid UNHCR documents.
The refugees said they had traveled to the UNHCR office after being driven out of their homes by local residents in the northern state of Penang on Sunday, and were seeking advice on resettlement, Reuters reported.
The news agency cited Penang police as saying that the Rohingya had “voluntarily moved” to Kuala Lumpur ​with the assistance of state and federal authorities.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said yesterday that he had directed police and immigration authorities to “take firm action” against the refugees in order “to control the situation and ensure public peace is maintained.” In an accompanying video, he said, “No one has the right to take over any part of the city.”
The incident comes amid a rising tide of popular hostility and online hate speech toward Rohingya refugees. Last month, more than half a million people signed a petition on Change.org calling for the removal of Rohingya refugees from Malaysia, which followed an outraged online response to cows being slaughtered by Rohingya refugees for the festival of Eid al-Adha. Prominent public figures have since described the Rohingya as “criminals” and “intruders” and likened them to a “cancer” on the country, while social media posts have encouraged violence against the Rohingya or encouraged users to report the locations of Rohingya refugees to the authorities.
Rohingya asylum seekers have arrived in Malaysia steadily over the past two decades, and particularly since 2017, when an ethnic cleansing campaign by the Myanmar military pushed more than 740,000 from Rakhine State into Bangladesh. Around 126,000 Rohingya are currently registered with UNHCR, more than half of the total, but Malaysia does not recognize the Rohingya as refugees, and, in line with the growing public hostility, has in recent years tightened the enforcement of its immigration laws against them.
Last week, Malaysia ordered UNHCR to temporarily stop registering new refugees in the country, as it begins operating its own system for managing asylum-seekers. The system, known as DPP, is set to apply much more stringent criteria than UNHCR about who can be granted refugee status in the country.
In this context, the online hate campaign has led to growing government scrutiny of Rohingya communities, and prompted investigations, raids, and the closures of Rohingya-linked schools and businesses, Reuters reported yesterday. At least nine Rohingya schools have so far been forced to shut nationwide, it stated, many of them because of rising harassment and abuse, including of children.
According to Malaysian media reports, the group of Rohingya that was detained outside the UNHCR office had been forced to leave their settlement in the village of Kuala Muda in Penang on Sunday. The New Straits Times reported that around 500 Rohingya vacated the village “peacefully”, “after villagers, authorities and members of the refugee community honored a month-long agreement to relocate.” It said that while the community “rarely caused problems,” the arrival of around 25 Rohingya a few months ago had prompted villagers to intervene.
“This transfer was carried out due to economic and territorial competition that arose ​following an increase in the Rohingya population in the area,” Seberang Perai Utara district police chief Anuar Abdul Rahman said in a statement quoted by Reuters.
While local officials said that there was “no riots, arguments, or violence” during the Rohingyas’ departure, one journalist posted on X that Kuala Muda had subsequently declared itself a “Rohingya-free area.”
As Alex Howlett reported for The Diplomat recently, the online hate campaign against the Rohingya has centered on similar narratives that accompanied their expulsion from Rakhine State in Myanmar – in particular, the toxic notion that Rohingya families reproduce at a far faster rate than Malaysian families.
Another parallel is the accusation that big social media companies, including Facebook’s parent company Meta, have failed to take quick enough action on hate speech posted on their platforms. A spokesperson for the advocacy group Article 19, which has previously expressed its concerns about the surge in hate speech against Rohingya, told Reuters that despite their policies on harmful content, enforcement by firms such as Meta and TikTok is inconsistent, while their AI moderation tools often allow hateful content to slip through the cracks.
Facebook in particular has been accused of failing to curb the spread of hateful speech in the run-up to the mass expulsion of Rohingya from Myanmar in 2017. Indeed, one group of Rohingya survivors initiated a class action against Meta in 2021, arguing that Facebook helped spread hate speech, misinformation, and incitement to violence and thereby “amounted to a substantial cause, and eventual perpetuation of, the Rohingya genocide.” The case was dismissed by a U.S. court in April.
Human rights groups have since condemned the Malaysian government’s detention of the Rohingya and called for greater protections of the vulnerable population. Bryony Lau, ‌deputy Asia ⁠director at Human Rights Watch, said that the Malaysian authorities “should prioritize protecting refugees who have been evicted from their homes instead of terrifying them further by detaining them.”
Amnesty International Malaysia’s spokesperson Divya Shesshsan Balakrishnan added, “Malaysia cannot build a credible refugee protection system while simultaneously treating refugees as people to be rounded up, detained, and removed.”
Malaysian authorities yesterday detained more than 100 Rohingya Muslim asylum seekers who had ‌gathered outside the office of the United Nations refugee agency in Kuala Lumpur, after being evicted from their settlement in the northern state of Penang.
According to a report by the New Straits Times, the group was transferred in four police vehicles from outside the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) at around 8:20 p.m. yesterday, along with “luggage and personal belongings.”
The paper today quoted Kuala Lumpur police chief Fadil Marsus as saying that 113 refugees, including 110 Rohingya, were being held at police headquarters. Fadil also said checks conducted during the documentation process at the police headquarters found that all the Rohingya refugees possessed valid UNHCR documents.
The refugees said they had traveled to the UNHCR office after being driven out of their homes by local residents in the northern state of Penang on Sunday, and were seeking advice on resettlement, Reuters reported.
The news agency cited Penang police as saying that the Rohingya had “voluntarily moved” to Kuala Lumpur ​with the assistance of state and federal authorities.
Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said yesterday that he had directed police and immigration authorities to “take firm action” against the refugees in order “to control the situation and ensure public peace is maintained.” In an accompanying video, he said, “No one has the right to take over any part of the city.”
The incident comes amid a rising tide of popular hostility and online hate speech toward Rohingya refugees. Last month, more than half a million people signed a petition on Change.org calling for the removal of Rohingya refugees from Malaysia, which followed an outraged online response to cows being slaughtered by Rohingya refugees for the festival of Eid al-Adha. Prominent public figures have since described the Rohingya as “criminals” and “intruders” and likened them to a “cancer” on the country, while social media posts have encouraged violence against the Rohingya or encouraged users to report the locations of Rohingya refugees to the authorities.
Rohingya asylum seekers have arrived in Malaysia steadily over the past two decades, and particularly since 2017, when an ethnic cleansing campaign by the Myanmar military pushed more than 740,000 from Rakhine State into Bangladesh. Around 126,000 Rohingya are currently registered with UNHCR, more than half of the total, but Malaysia does not recognize the Rohingya as refugees, and, in line with the growing public hostility, has in recent years tightened the enforcement of its immigration laws against them.
Last week, Malaysia ordered UNHCR to temporarily stop registering new refugees in the country, as it begins operating its own system for managing asylum-seekers. The system, known as DPP, is set to apply much more stringent criteria than UNHCR about who can be granted refugee status in the country.
In this context, the online hate campaign has led to growing government scrutiny of Rohingya communities, and prompted investigations, raids, and the closures of Rohingya-linked schools and businesses, Reuters reported yesterday. At least nine Rohingya schools have so far been forced to shut nationwide, it stated, many of them because of rising harassment and abuse, including of children.
According to Malaysian media reports, the group of Rohingya that was detained outside the UNHCR office had been forced to leave their settlement in the village of Kuala Muda in Penang on Sunday. The New Straits Times reported that around 500 Rohingya vacated the village “peacefully”, “after villagers, authorities and members of the refugee community honored a month-long agreement to relocate.” It said that while the community “rarely caused problems,” the arrival of around 25 Rohingya a few months ago had prompted villagers to intervene.
articles.summary: The detention of the group, who were reportedly driven out of a settlement in Penang on Sunday, comes amid rising public hostility toward Rohingya refugees.

articles.title: The Shifting Contours of Transnational Cybercrime in the Asia-Pacific
articles.full_text:
A conversation with Bangkok-based anti-fraud advisor Ian Timberlake.
Retired journalist and advisor on financial crime Ian Timberlake.
Last week, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) released its latest report on transnational scam networks, which found that victims from East Asia, Southeast Asia, Australia, and New Zealand had been defrauded of up to $114.1 billion in 2025.
The report draws on official data, case records, financial intelligence, and field research in describing an increasingly sophisticated criminal ecosystem dominated by Chinese-origin transnational organized crime groups.
It also covers the trafficking of physical goods and services, including wildlife, along with cyber-enabled fraud, criminal infrastructure, and platform-based financial settlements.
Ian Timberlake, a retired journalist who acts as a part-time adviser on anti-money laundering and financial crime, attended the launch of the 256-page UNODC report in Bangkok and the expert discussions that followed.
In the latest edition of the Beyond the Mekong podcast, he speaks with The Diplomat’s Luke Hunt about the spread of industrialized scamming and fraud across the region, from Sri Lanka to Timor-Leste.
AI is also playing a role in the scam economy, with deep fakes being deployed to defraud banks, financial institutions, and ordinary people, at a level that is challenging international law enforcement agencies and their governments.
Timberlake worked as a journalist for 39 years, initially in his native Canada, focusing mostly on crime and police reporting. He also spent 26 years as a correspondent and editor with the Agence France-Presse news agency in Asia, the Middle East, Africa, and Washington, D.C.
He is a member of the Association of Certified Anti-Money Laundering Specialists and the author of “The Bay Man from Bulawayo,” available on Rakuten Kobo.

articles.title: Resignation of Bank Indonesia Governor Shocks Markets, Raises Independence Questions
articles.full_text:
Perry Warjiyo, who has served as governor of the central bank since 2018, said that he was stepping down for “personal reasons.”
Bank Indonesia Governor Perry Warjiyo (right) and Indonesian Finance Minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati speak during a G20 press briefing during the 2022 Annual Meetings at the International Monetary Fund in Washington, D.C., Oct. 13, 2022.
The governor of Bank Indonesia (BI) stepped down from his post yesterday, sending a tremor through markets and prompting fresh concerns about political interference in economic policymaking.
During a press conference, State Secretariat Minister Prasetyo Hadi announced Perry Warjiyo’s resignation, which comes two years before the expiry of his current term as BI governor.
“As of yesterday, we officially received a letter of resignation from the Governor of BI to the President,” Prasetyo said during the press conference, accompanied by members of the BI Board of Governors, the state news agency Antara reported.
“The president accepted Perry Warjiyo’s resignation and conveyed his utmost gratitude for his dedication in leading Bank Indonesia for seven years,” he added.
Perry began his career at BI in 1984, and has served as governor since 2018. He cited only “personal reasons” for stepping down and did not meet President Prabowo Subianto directly before submitting his resignation, Prasetyo said.
He added that Senior Deputy Governor Destry Damayanti, a former chief economist at Bank Mandiri, would serve as acting governor until a replacement governor is elected. This candidate would be chosen from a list of three candidates proposed by Prabowo, which would be forward to parliament for a “fit and proper test.” Legislators would then select one of the candidates.
Perry’s departure comes at a difficult time for the Indonesian economy. The country’s currency fell to record lows this year, passing the psychological threshold of 18,000 rupiah to the U.S. dollar in June. It is now trading at a lower level than at any time since the Asian Financial Crisis of 1997-1998.
The unexpected resignation set off a minor tremor in Indonesian markets. The Jakarta Stock Exchange Composite Index fell 0.5 per cent, and the rupiah slumped from around 17,935 to the U.S. dollar to 18,009 by the close of trading yesterday.
The bigger issue is how Perry’s resignation might compound investors’ growing skepticism about the Prabowo administration’s economic stewardship.
BI has been under pressure to support Prabowo’s economic policy, which aims to achieve an annual GDP growth of 8 percent per year for the rest of his term. This has included high-spending populist policies, including a multibillion-dollar free meal program, which have widened the fiscal deficit and pushed it toward its legally mandated ceiling of 3 percent of GDP. The former general has also increased the state’s involvement in the Indonesian economy in a bid to maximize the country’s return from natural resources and international trade.
These policies, along with the firing of respected Finance Minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati last September, have unsettled investors and undermined Indonesia’s hard-won reputation for fiscal conservatism.
In March, both Moody’s and Fitch announced ratings outlook downgrades for Indonesia, with the latter citing the “increasing ⁠policy uncertainty and erosion of Indonesia’s policy mix consistency and credibility” and the “growing centralization of policymaking authority.” This came shortly after the global index provider MSCI threatened to downgrade Indonesia to “frontier market” status due to a number of transparency concerns in its stock market, including the high concentration of ownership in certain companies and the limited “free float” of shares. MSCI will announce its verdict in November.
Perry’s surprise exit only compounds these concerns, and investors will be watching closely to see who is chosen to replace him. As Channel News Asia reported, “the majority of his five deputies are long-time central bankers with at least 30 years of experience working for Bank Indonesia.”
One of the exceptions is Thomas Djiwandono, 54, a former journalist, financial analyst, consultant, and politician for the Gerindra Party, who also happens to be a nephew of President Prabowo. Prabowo appointed Djiwandono as deputy finance minister in October 2024. He then nominated him as BI deputy governor in February of this year, an appointment that prompted concerns about nepotism and political influence over BI. While Prabowo has not given any indication that he wishes to appoint his nephew to lead the central bank, the question is likely to linger over the transition period.
Indonesian media outlets have reported recently that Prabowo may also look beyond BI for the central bank’s next governor, with current Finance Minister Purbaya Yudhi Sadewa a potential candidate, CNA reported.
While the Indonesian government said that the leadership transition at BI would not disrupt monetary ​policy or economic stability, and Interim Governor Destry said yesterday that the central bank would “always ensure the continuity of its duties,” the Prabowo administration will have to go to extra lengths to overcome the perception of political interference.
“What must now be anticipated after Perry’s resignation is the weakening of Bank Indonesia’s independence,” Bhima Yudhistira ⁠Adhinegara, executive director of the Center of Economic and Law Studies, told Reuters. “Restoring investor confidence will certainly not be easy, especially since the direction of monetary policy is ​under executive control.”

articles.title: The Limits of China’s Growing Influence at the United Nations
articles.full_text:
Beijing’s engagement is more cautious, selective, and constrained than it appears.
Chinese President Xi Jinping speaks during the U.N. General Assembly’s 70th session, Sep. 28, 2015.
The United Nations has been undergoing its most significant overhaul in history, the UN80 initiative, which aims to review mandates, reduce costs, and consider structural changes across the system. This is partly due to mounting arrears, of which more than 95 percent of what is owed to the regular U.N. budget is owed by the United States, historically the organization’s largest financial contributor. In January, Secretary-General António Guterres warned that the U.N. faced “imminent financial collapse,” with long-lasting impact on its global operations.
As the United States becomes a less reliable funder, a tempting assumption has taken hold, that China will step into the space left by Washington. The logic appears straightforward. Against the backdrop of China-U.S. competition and Beijing’s growing ambition in global governance. China routinely presents itself as a defender of true multilateralism. It has become the second-largest contributor to the U.N. regular and peacekeeping budgets and has sought greater representation in international organizations. As Washington turns away from the U.N., Beijing seemingly has both the ambition and the opportunity to take its place.
But China’s pursuit of greater influence should not be mistaken for an attempt to replace the United States. Beijing wants a greater voice at the U.N., but it has shown little willingness to assume the open-ended responsibilities that U.S. leadership has historically entailed. Its engagement is better understood as cautious, selective, and bounded by what Chinese officials repeatedly described as acting “within its own capacity” (力所能及).
China’s rhetorical commitment to the United Nations is real. Chinese officials consistently call for upholding the U.N. Charter, strengthening the organization’s authority, and defending a U.N.-centered international system. Yet its defense of the U.N. is neither novel nor unconditional. Since recovering its seat in 1971, Beijing has regarded the U.N. as an important arena in which it can constrain U.S. hegemony, defend state sovereignty, and amplify the voice of developing countries. Its current rhetoric intensifies this established position rather than marking a wholesale transformation in China’s international role. As the United States has withdrawn from international bodies and reduced multilateral funding, Beijing has used this language to contrast its professed support for multilateralism with Washington’s unilateralism.
Moreover, the other side of the rhetoric is often neglected. Alongside Beijing’s call for stronger U.N.-centered multilateralism, China routinely promises to contribute according to its capabilities. The “within its capacity” narrative presents China as a responsible power while preserving considerable discretion over the scale, timing, and destination of its commitments. 
China’s financial record reflects precisely this balance. Its assessed contribution has risen dramatically alongside its economic weight. Under the scale of assessments adopted for 2025 to 2027, China accounts for around 20 percent of the U.N. regular budget, ranking just behind the U.S. at 22 percent. China is also the second-largest contributor to U.N. peacekeeping. These figures are frequently cited as evidence that Beijing is poised to displace Washington at the organization. 
But assessed contributions tell only part of the story. They are obligations calculated according to an agreed formula, not straightforward measures of a government’s willingness to finance international leadership. The sharper test of Beijing’s intentions is voluntary funding, particularly the earmarked contributions, through which donors can earmark this money for particular organizations, countries, sectors, or projects, allowing them to translate funding into policy influence. Much of the U.N. system, particularly its development and humanitarian operations, largely depends on earmarked contributions. 
The United States has long been the largest source of earmarked funding, whereas China has not come close to matching it. According to data from the U.N. System Chief Executives Board for Coordination, Washington provided approximately $10.5 billion in earmarked contributions in 2024. China provided about $225.5 million, just over 2 percent of the U.S. total. Although Beijing’s earmarked contributions have grown, they have increased from a low base and remain modest relative to the size of its economy and its mandatory payments. 
The difference is not merely quantitative. Beijing also allocates its voluntary funding selectively. It favors institutions and programs that align with its policy priorities or create opportunities to demonstrate its preferred approach to development cooperation. Research also finds that Beijing tends to avoid organizations already heavily shaped by U.S. funding and personnel. This selectivity allows China to pursue influence where the expected political returns are greater while limiting the costs of direct competition. 
China’s personnel presence exhibits a similar tension. Beijing has sought to increase the number of Chinese nationals working in international organizations and has campaigned for Chinese candidates to lead specialized agencies, such as the Food and Agriculture Organization. Its efforts have produced visible results, but progress in selected organizations and leadership positions should not be mistaken for institutional dominance. In 2025, 1,641 Chinese nationals worked across the U.N. system, compared with more than 5,074 U.S. nationals. China therefore remained underrepresented in U.N. staffing relative to the size of its population and financial contributions. A small number of senior appointments cannot immediately create the deep pool of international civil servants, technical specialists, diplomatic networks, and institutional experience accumulated by established powers over decades.
China’s foreign aid bureaucracy also constrains a rapid expansion of multilateral financing. The China International Development Cooperation Agency (CIDCA) was established partly to improve coordination, but other ministries and financial institutions retain important implementation and funding responsibilities. CIDCA’s lower bureaucratic rank and lack of implementation authority could generate continued friction with other ministries, especially the Ministries of Commerce and Foreign Affairs. This fragmented structure is better suited to negotiating bounded projects and designated funds than to supplying large amounts of flexible financing across the U.N. system. 
There is also an identity constraint. China continues to present itself as the world’s largest developing country and a partner in South-South cooperation. This positioning allows Beijing to claim solidarity with the developing world and resist expectations that its international obligations should mirror those of the U.S. Replacing Washington financially would weaken that distinction and invite demands that China assume responsibilities it has long argued should remain differentiated.
China’s domestic economic constraints further reinforce this cautious approach. Fiscal pressures and competing domestic priorities make it politically less attractive for Beijing to assume substantially larger international expenditures, particularly when many of the benefits would be diffuse and difficult to demonstrate to its domestic audience. 
None of this means that the U.S. retreat will leave China without new opportunities. Beijing does not need to replace U.S. funding dollar-for-dollar to gain influence. As U.N. agencies become more financially vulnerable, even relatively modest Chinese contributions may acquire greater political weight. Institutions working in areas aligned with China’s priorities may attract additional attention or project funding. Beijing, for example, pledged $500 million to the World Health Organization after the United States announced its withdrawal. China’s selective engagement could therefore change the distribution of resources across the U.N. system without resolving its underlying financial crisis.
This prospect should concern both U.N. officials and U.S. policymakers. Washington’s withdrawal will not simply transfer responsibility to its principal competitor. It will create gaps that Beijing can exploit selectively but is unlikely to fill. China can benefit from a U.S. retreat without repairing the damage that retreat causes. It may acquire a larger voice in selected institutions while the wider system loses budgets, programs and operational capacity.

articles.title: India Successfully Tests Kusha Long-range Surface-to-Air Missile
articles.full_text:
This is an important milestone in India’s evolving multi-layered long-range air defense architecture envisaged under Mission Sudarshan Chakra.
The maiden flight test of the long-range surface-to-air Kusha missile from the APJ Abdul Kalam Island off the coast of Odisha, India, July 23,2026.
On July 23, India’s Defense Research and Development Organization (DRDO) successfully carried out the maiden test of the M1 long-range surface-to-air missile (SAM), one of three interceptors being developed under the Kusha program, from the APJ Abdul Kalam Island off the Odisha coast. This is an important milestone in India’s evolving multi-layered long-range air defense architecture envisaged under Mission Sudarshan Chakra that is scheduled to be put in place by 2035.
This test was conducted against an electronic target simulating a high-speed and high-altitude aerial threat, which was successfully intercepted. DRDO said that the Kusha missile system is capable of “neutralizing wide variety of aerial threats including fighter jets, missiles, UAVs and large enemy aircrafts within a wide range and altitude envelope.”
Calling the test flight an “important milestone” in Indian defense research and development, India’s Defense Minister Rajnath Singh observed that only a handful of nations possess the capability of developing a long-range SAM system.
Under Project Kusha, DRDO is developing three long-range interceptors – M1 to engage targets up to 150 km, M2 with a range of 250 km, and M3 to engage targets at distances of 350-400 km. The kill vehicle will remain the same, with a booster added to augment the range. Development is expected to be completed in the next couple of years, with induction targeted by 2030. Defense public sector undertaking Bharat Dynamics Limited and Solar Industries are the chosen Development-cum-Production Partners and are involved in the process. Bharat Electronics Limited is the development partner with DRDO for different types of radars and control systems.
The system is backed by an architecture of command-and-control systems, a variety of radars, sensors, and various missile systems all plugged into the Integrated Air Command and Control System (IACCS) of the Indian Air Force. The Indian Army’s and Navy’s air defense networks are also linked to the IACCS to form a comprehensive air defense picture of the country’s airspace and to look deep into airspace far beyond the borders to track incoming threats.
India’s long-range air defense is currently based on the Russian S-400 Triumf systems, which have an interception range of 400 km. Five S-400 regiments were contracted under a $5.43 billion deal with Russia in 2018. However, deliveries have been significantly delayed with the fourth regiment now delivered and the fifth to be delivered by year-end.
After the four-day military conflict with Pakistan under Operation Sindoor in May 2025, the Defense Ministry approved the procurement of five additional S-400 regiments for which negotiations are underway. S-400 had proven its worth during Operation Sindoor and not only in shooting down incoming projectiles – it was also employed in an offensive role to shoot down a Pakistani early warning aircraft over 300 km away.
Much has been written in the last few days about how Project Kusha will reduce import dependence on the S-400. Technically yes, but it’s a very long way off, as earlier contracted regiments are still being inducted and a new contract is in the pipeline, which means deliveries and inductions are several years away. So once Project Kusha starts getting deployed, for the near-to-medium future it will complement the S-400 and work in tandem to provide India a seamless air defense cover, particularly building redundancy. Nonetheless, it is a critical domain to build self-reliance.
Long-range interceptors give additional time to respond, especially given the short distances on India’s Western border, allowing threats to be neutralized far away from population clusters or high-value assets.
Apart from emerging threats, India faces a persistent threat from medium and long-range ballistic missiles of Pakistan and China, its nuclear-armed adversaries on the western and northern fronts, respectively. Hence, an anti-ballistic missile shield is critical.
The S-400 is designed to engage a wide range of threats, including tactical and theatre ballistic missiles and medium-range ballistic missiles, while Project Kusha is expected to be able to tackle certain classes of ballistic and hypersonic threats.
For the larger threat envelope, India has developed an indigenous Anti-Ballistic Missile defense; Phase-I, designed to engage ballistic missiles with a range of up to 2000 kms, has been validated and Phase-II for missiles of up to 5000 kms, is under development.
After the 400 km S-400, the next system currently in the tier is the Barak-8 or Medium Range-SAM with a range of 70 km, jointly developed with Israel Aerospace Industry (IAI). That’s a significant gap in the missile ranges and the three interceptors under Project Kusha will bridge the gap once deployed, creating a truly multi-layered long-range net.
The Naval variant of the Barak-8 is called LR-SAM and the land variant MR-SAM. At the shorter range are the Akash indigenous systems and the Israeli Spyder quick reaction systems.
According to officials involved in the Kusha project, the entire project, including seekers, actuators, and computing systems, is indigenous. This test was conducted against an electronic target simulating a high-speed and high-altitude aerial threat, which was successfully intercepted. DRDO said that the Kusha missile system is capable of “neutralizing wide variety of aerial threats including fighter jets, missiles, UAVs and large enemy aircrafts within a wide range and altitude envelope.”
Calling the test flight an “important milestone” in Indian defense research and development, India’s Defense Minister Rajnath Singh observed that only a handful of nations possess the capability of developing a long-range SAM system.
Under Project Kusha, DRDO is developing three long-range interceptors – M1 to engage targets up to 150 km, M2 with a range of 250 km, and M3 to engage targets at distances of 350-400 km. Defense public sector undertaking Bharat Dynamics Limited and Solar Industries are the chosen Development-cum-Production Partners and are involved in the process. Bharat Electronics Limited is the development partner with DRDO for different types of radars and control systems.
The system is backed by an architecture of command-and-control systems, a variety of radars, sensors, and various missile systems all plugged into the Integrated Air Command and Control System (IACCS) of the Indian Air Force. The Indian Army’s and Navy’s air defense networks are also linked to the IACCS to form a comprehensive air defense picture of the country’s airspace and to look deep into airspace far beyond the borders to track incoming threats.

After the four-day military conflict with Pakistan under Operation Sindoor in May 2025, the Defense Ministry approved the procurement of five additional S-400 regiments for which negotiations are underway. S-400 had proven its worth during Operation Sindoor and not only in shooting down incoming projectiles – it was also employed in an offensive role to shoot down a Pakistani early warning aircraft over 300 km away.
Much has been written in the last few days about how Project Kusha will reduce import dependence on the S-400. Technically yes, but it’s a very long way off, as earlier contracted regiments are still being inducted and a new contract is in the pipeline, which means deliveries and inductions are several years away. articles.title: China, Japan, and the Memory Security Dilemma
articles.full_text:
How historical memory distorts strategic signaling in Sino-Japanese relations.
In April 2026, a Murakami-class Japanese Maritime Self-Defense Force (MSDF) destroyer transited the Taiwan Strait. Such passages have become more frequent amid rising tensions over Taiwan since 2025. Yet this instance triggered an unusually strong reaction from China. The reason was not the transit itself, but its timing. It occurred on April 17, the anniversary of the 1895 Treaty of Shimonoseki, which ended the First Sino-Japanese War. In Chinese historical narratives, the Treaty of Shimonoseki is part of the “Century of Humiliation.”
Chinese commentators quickly interpreted the timing as deliberate. Some viewed it as a symbolic reminder of imperial victory. Others saw it as a signal of strategic intent toward Taiwan. Japanese officials offered no indication that the date carried symbolic meaning. It may have been coincidence. But the dispute highlights a deeper structural problem in East Asian security. States do not only react to actions; they react to meanings. And increasingly, those meanings are determined not by present behavior but by historical memory.
For decades, analysts have explained East Asian tensions through familiar geopolitical factors: military modernization, alliance politics, maritime disputes, and Taiwan’s strategic importance. These remain essential, but they can’t fully explain why relatively minor events generate outsized political controversies between China and Japan.
Historical memory has become a strategic variable. It shapes how governments and publics interpret policy behavior. It determines which signals are perceived, which explanations appear credible, and which intentions are considered plausible.
Under conditions of declining trust, historical memory transforms ambiguity into meaning, coincidence into strategy, and routine behavior into evidence of hostility. This produces what can be called a “memory security dilemma”: a condition in which historical memory systematically amplifies strategic mistrust, leading states to perceive hostile intent beyond what is intended. Unlike the traditional security dilemma, which arises from uncertainty about capabilities and intentions, this one arises from uncertainty about meaning.
International relations theory has long emphasized misperception. States rarely know each other’s intentions with certainty. As Robert Jervis and others have argued, policymakers tend to infer coherence where none exists, connecting isolated events into narratives of strategy.
The traditional security dilemma builds on this logic: defensive actions are interpreted as offensive preparations, producing spirals of mistrust. But in the context of Sino-Japanese relations today, a deeper layer is emerging. Strategic competition is increasingly filtered through historical narratives that shape interpretation of other states’ actions.
The traditional security dilemma is about uncertainty over intentions. The memory security dilemma is about uncertainty over meaning. An action may be fully understood in operational terms while still being misread in symbolic terms. History becomes a cognitive shortcut that fills interpretive gaps. As trust declines, this shortcut becomes dominant. States rely less on present evidence and more on historical analogy to interpret behavior.
The memory security dilemma is most visible in Sino-Japanese relations because the two countries do not remember the same past in the same way. In China, modern history is politically central. Events such as the Treaty of Shimonoseki (April 17, 1895), the Manchurian Incident (September 18, 1931), and the Marco Polo Bridge Incident (July 7, 1937) remain embedded in education, commemorations, and national identity narratives. They are not simply historical references. They function as interpretive frameworks linking past vulnerability to present strategic concerns.
Japan’s memory structure is different. While wartime history has been extensively debated, specific dates tied to Chinese historical trauma are not equally salient in public consciousness and school education. Many Japanese policymakers would not immediately recognize the symbolic resonance in China of dates like July 7, April 17 or September 18. 
The April 2026 MSDF destroyer passage incident was not the only example of this historical perception gap in the context of China-Japan relations. For instance, on July 7, 2012, Japan’s then-Prime Minister Noda Yoshihiko announced the government would be nationalizing the Diaoyu/Senkaku Islands. Making such an announcement on that sensitive date was bound to heighten concerns on the Chinese side. 
According to a retrospective analysis by Moriyasu Hiroshi, editorial board member of Kyodo News, the Noda administration had actually finalized the policy on July 6. However, after The Asahi Shimbun broke the story on July 7, the government had little choice but to confirm the report that same day. Neither The Asahi Shimbun nor Japanese government officials appeared to recognize that July 7 carries a profound historical significance in the collective historical memory of China. As a result, they inadvertently deepened the suspicion from Beijing.
This asymmetry of China-Japan memory feeds into Beijing’s threat perceptions. The same event may appear ordinary in Tokyo but politically charged in Beijing. One side sees no signal, the other sees proactive signaling. Misunderstanding does not arise from disagreement over facts, but from disagreement over whether meaning exists in the historical context.
The April 2026 MSDF transit of the Taiwan Strait illustrates how this dynamic operates in practice. From an operational perspective, the transit was consistent with established patterns of Japanese maritime activity since 2024. But this time, the specific timing transformed China’s interpretation. 
Because the transit coincided with a historically sensitive anniversary in Chinese historical memory, it was read by some Chinese observers as symbolic action rather than routine behavior. Once such interpretations enter public discourse, they become self-reinforcing. Future actions are interpreted through the same framework, regardless of intent. Each perceived signal strengthens prior belief, narrowing interpretive flexibility. Over time, perception begins to drive strategic reality. 
The danger of the memory security dilemma in Sin0-Japanese relations is its self-reinforcing structure. Japanese policymakers may be entirely unaware that a certain date has any symbolic meaning in China. Chinese observers may over-interpret those same actions because they are embedded in a highly charged historical narrative. 
Neither side is necessarily acting irrationally, but the outcome is escalating mistrust as perceived hostility generates defensive responses. Those responses are then cited as confirmation of the original suspicion. The cycle reinforces itself. As this loop continues, the gap between intended meaning and perceived meaning widens – even if material behavior remains stable. The security competition becomes less about power shifts and more about accumulated misinterpretation.
The challenge is not to remove history from politics. That is neither possible nor desirable. The challenge is to manage how history is used to interpret the present. This requires strategic empathy: the ability to anticipate how actions will be interpreted through another society’s historical experience. 
For Japan, this means recognizing that operational decisions may carry unintended historical resonance in China and avoid the conduction of China-related policy on historically sensitive dates. For China, it means recognizing that timing is not always signaling; sometimes it’s merely a coincidence. China should avoid overinterpreting Japanese intentions for its current foreign and security policy.

articles.title: India’s Gen Z Protesters Score Major Victory Against Modi Government
articles.full_text:
After angry students forced the education minister to resign, Prime Minister Modi’s aura of invincibility has been dented.
Protesters at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, including Cockroach Janta Party founder, Abhijeet Dibke (in yellow T-shirt), celebrate the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan on July 25, 2026.
Twelve years into the Narendra Modi-led Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government in New Delhi, and the unthinkable happened.
A minister in the Union Cabinet, Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, was forced to resign under massive pressure from student protesters demanding “accountability” for the leak of question papers for the National Eligibility cum Entrance Tests (NEET) on May 3.
Pradhan’s resignation came 36 days after the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) launched its indefinite mass protests at New Delhi’s Jantar Mantar calling for exactly that outcome. It is a major victory for the CJP, an online satirical campaign started by Abhijeet Dipke in May 2026, in response to a derisive comment by the chief justice of India equating unemployed youth to cockroaches. Dipke’s online campaign went viral, garnering an online support base of over 2 million.
But few would have expected then that the CJP, which morphed from an online protest into a mass Gen Z protest on June 6, would force the Modi government to bend.
Since 2014, when the Modi-led BJP came to power backed by an overwhelming majority, his government has ruled with an iron hand, crushing all forms of dissent and ruthlessly targeting its opponents, be it opposition politicians or others. Three successive election victories had further cemented the perception that the Modi government was invincible.
That aura of invincibility, carefully cultivated for over a decade, has now cracked, with Gen Z students forcing Pradhan to step down.
The CJP’S first reaction on X (formerly Twitter) to the minister’s resignation was clear: “Democracy Wins.”
“I am a Cockroach,” a 20-year-old student protester in Kolkata told The Diplomat,. “We students had one main demand — accountability. And we have achieved that,” she said, elated over Pradhan’s resignation.
India’s Gen Z protest has succeeded in introducing the word “accountability” into the political discourse in the country. Under Modi and his confidante Home Minister Amit Shah, accountability had practically disappeared.
In 2015, when the Congress Party called for the resignation of then-Foreign Minister Sushma Swaraj for facilitating fugitive Lalit Modi’s travel papers to Portugal, Defense Minister Rajnath Singh said: “This is not the UPA government, this is the NDA government. Ministers do not resign here.” BJP leaders repeated this thereafter to fend off demands for a minister’s resignation. Accepting moral responsibility is perceived by the BJP as a sign of weakness.
This was not the case when the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance was in power (2009-2014) and the BJP, then in opposition, demanded and secured the resignation of several top Congress ministers. Unlike the UPA, Modi and the BJP did not, at any cost, want to set a precedent in which cabinet ministers would be held liable for actions under their government’s watch.
Before Pradhan, the only minister in the Modi government to have resigned was M. J. Akbar, the junior foreign minister in 2018, who was accused of sexual harassment during his time as an editor.
The Gen Z protesters were undeterred by the BJP’s rigid reluctance to take responsibility for scams and scandals. Fixing “accountability” was a buzzword during the protests. The CJP wanted authorities to be held responsible, especially for the 21 students who took their lives following the NEET paper leak.
Over the past decade, the Modi-Shah duo had managed to quell agitations and topple governments in opposition-ruled states. It used central agencies to intimidate opposition politicians into joining the BJP. This template had succeeded in providing stability to the BJP-led National Democratic Alliance government, in office since 2014.
Many commentators have noted that Gen Z is fearless and irreverent as a generation. It doesn’t care for nor worship those in authority. Unfettered by concepts like “respect for elders” that limited millennials when dealing with authority, Gen Z speaks without fear.
In response to the paper leaks, Modi called on his ministers to “get more active on Instagram,” as if that was a solution to the problem. Dipke wrote on X, “This is why a PM should be educated,” a reference to Modi’s lack of education.
The biggest casualty of the protests is Modi’s strong man image. The Modi regime and Modi himself had gone to great lengths to conjure an image of him being almost “non-biological,” with a manly “56-inch chest,” a heroic figure within the country and much-sought after leader abroad.
Gen Z lampooned this personality cult through slogans, memes, and limericks, poking fun at the “56-inch small monkey” and heckling him to flee.
While the CJP’s stated demand was for the education minister’s resignation, it was Modi who was the target of songs, slogans, reels, posters, memes, and graffiti. Modi’s image has taken a beating. This possibly hastened the government’s decision to concede the protesters’ demand.
This does not bode well for the Modi–Shah regime.
Modi was among the first Indian leaders to leverage social media, which played an important role in his coming to power in 2014. He has often gloated about his huge following on social media. Gen Z have now used the same social media space and mainly Instagram to demolish Modi’s strong man image.
The other big takeaway of the Gen Z victory has been the discrediting of the BJP’s media management framework. The BJP’s control of the news media, especially TV channels, which have a wide audience outreach, has played an important role in disseminating propaganda so far.  But this “lap dog media” was thoroughly discredited by the protesters. The latter did not allow them to set the narrative, and even though news channels tried to defame the protesters as anti-nationals, funded by foreign agencies, peopled by vandals and thugs, the students fought back by posting reels and real-time videos, showing the real picture on the ground.
The stark difference was evident, especially when the government brutally cracked down on the protesters on July 20. While pro-government channels portrayed it as violence by students, independent journalists laid bare the inhumane use of pellet guns and batons on students, leaving them with bloody injuries. In fact, this use of excessive force boomeranged on the regime, drawing in sympathizers ranging from cinema actors to opposition leaders.
The government’s media management strategy in response to the farmer protests of 2021, the anti-CAA protests of 2019-20, and other protests did not work this time around. Even the BJP’s “IT cell,” which relentlessly trolls opposition protests, proved no match for Gen Z creativity.
The Modi regime’s inability to gauge or tackle Gen Z anger stands exposed.
Youth account for 30 percent of India’s electorate. The Modi government cannot afford to ignore student frustration with the education system and unemployment — issues that it has been diverting attention from.
Twelve years into the Narendra Modi-led Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government in New Delhi, and the unthinkable happened.
A minister in the Union Cabinet, Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, was forced to resign under massive pressure from student protesters demanding “accountability” for the leak of question papers for the National Eligibility cum Entrance Tests (NEET) on May 3.
articles.summary: After angry students forced the education minister to resign, Prime Minister Modi’s aura of invincibility has been dented.

articles.title: New Global Trade Arrangement Gains Momentum – And It’s Worth Watching
articles.full_text:
The Future of Investment and Trade Partnership, with 19 members and counting, is championing open and fair trade at a time when others are retreating.
Ministers and delegates pose for a group photo at the Future of Investment and Trade Partnership meeting in Auckland, New Zealand, July 17, 2026.
On July 17, an important meeting on global trade and economic cooperation took place in New Zealand: Ministers and delegates from 21 countries across Asia, Latin America, Europe, the Pacific, the Middle East and Africa gathered to advance work on the Future of Investment and Trade Partnership (FIT-P). The meeting went largely unnoticed but deserves more attention.
FIT-P – an innovative trade arrangement where members agree to collaborate on strengthening supply chains, removing non-tariff barriers, integrating new technologies, and facilitating investment – is growing its membership, creating new models for cooperation, and building economic resilience in today’s turbulent trade world. Its economic heft may not be giant but this new group, representing close to 20 percent of global goods trade, is championing open and fair trade at a time when others are retreating. 
Launched in September 2025, this global initiative was spearheaded by four trade-dependent countries: Singapore, Switzerland, New Zealand, and the United Arab Emirates. Each of these core members quietly recruited some of their usual economic friends, and FIT-P landed on the world stage with 14 members, including Chile, Morocco, Norway, Uruguay, Rwanda and Brunei, which are eager to try something new.
 In the course of just 10 months, five new members have joined: Malaysia and Paraguay in November, and South Korea, Peru, and Thailand signing on at the recent Auckland meeting. Samoa and Fiji also attended the Auckland meeting as observers.
This momentum reflects a growing interest on the part of many countries in reaching for new instruments and new ways of working together in the midst of the myriad of global trade challenges countries face today. It also supports the new emphasis on trade diversification – a key pillar of many countries’ economic security and economic resilience strategies today. It doesn’t mean that these countries are necessarily moving away from the big economies of the United States, China, or the EU; rather it embodies the realities of today that having all your eggs in one or two baskets is not the best strategy for sustained economic growth.  
The world’s biggest economies are not a part of FIT-P, and this initiative may not be grabbing the headlines with new tariff rates or rules. In fact that is by design and possibly also part of its attraction. Its focus is on bringing small and medium-sized economies together to tackle the trade challenges of a modern world in creative and practical ways and enhance investment flows. Smaller countries are often nimbler, can adapt more quickly, and are more outward looking in their approach. This is not to say they are free from protectionist tendencies, but they usually recognize that they cannot solve all their problems and grow their economy to its full potential without access to and inputs from markets abroad.  
Furthermore, this is no ordinary free trade agreement – there are no legally binding obligations, and countries are not trading market access commitments. Instead, FIT-P is designed to be a dynamic platform where members pledge to adhere to the rules-based trading system and collaborate on specific, practical initiatives that facilitate trade and investment. 
Importantly, countries can pick and choose which specific FIT-P initiatives they sign up to.  When FIT-P was launched, the founding members used words like “agile,” “flexible,” and “adaptable” to describe their approach – not your usual terms for trade agreements. 
Reflecting this approach, the Auckland meeting concluded with three different declarations on practical steps to tackle non-tariff barriers, to harness the power of digital technology to facilitate trade, and to build economic resilience to address economic security risks. Various members signed up to each declaration separately.
This flexible approach may well be the direction we see more of in the future, especially given the difficulties the World Trade Organization (WTO) has in concluding agreements these days. While subsets of WTO members have embarked on plurilateral agreements on specific topics, like digital and investment facilitation, these agreements have met serious challenges in Geneva. The FIT-P approach reverses this sequent. Its members recognize from the get-go that not everyone will be joining all commitments – and this is part of the deal. It reflects a more practical way forward and ensures that those who are not ready to move forward with certain commitments do not hold back those who are ready.   
The FIT-P group also provides a new forum for countries that support open and rules-based trade to meet, to discuss the latest developments and challenges in the global trading order, and to develop effective responses – and fast. For small countries in particular, providing this space for discussion at the ministerial level, where creative ideas can be tested and hopefully flourish, is an important end goal in and of itself. 
This forum can also serve as a catalyst for broader multilateral action. For example, it may well be easier to first conclude commitments in certain areas among this smaller, trade-reliant group of countries, which can then, over time, be taken up by others.
At a time when the global trading order is under increasing strain, FIT-P appears to go against the grain, championing the rules-based system and the value of working together with smaller sets of countries. As its numbers grow, its “pick-and-choose” model for plurilateral trade partnerships serves as a useful test case for perhaps a more effective way to achieve increased economic integration.

On July 17, an important meeting on global trade and economic cooperation took place in New Zealand: Ministers and delegates from 21 countries across Asia, Latin America, Europe, the Pacific, the Middle East and Africa gathered to advance work on the Future of Investment and Trade Partnership (FIT-P). The meeting went largely unnoticed but deserves more attention.
FIT-P – an innovative trade arrangement where members agree to collaborate on strengthening supply chains, removing non-tariff barriers, integrating new technologies, and facilitating investment – is growing its membership, creating new models for cooperation, and building economic resilience in today’s turbulent trade world. Its economic heft may not be giant but this new group, representing close to 20 percent of global goods trade, is championing open and fair trade at a time when others are retreating.
articles.summary: The Future of Investment and Trade Partnership, with 19 members and counting, is championing open and fair trade at a time when others are retreating.

articles.title: Pakistan, China Sign $850 Million Deals to Boost Pharmaceutical Cooperation
articles.full_text:
The costs of Pakistan’s dependence on imports for medicines and vaccines are huge. Chinese investment could end this reliance.
Health workers vaccinate a 2-year-old child during a polio vaccination campaign in January 2015 in a rural area of Tehsil Fateh Jang, Punjab in Pakistan.
Last week, Pakistan and Chinese companies signed agreements worth $850 million at the Pakistan-China Pharmaceutical and Healthcare B2B Investment Conference in Islamabad.
Held on July 17 and 18, the event focused on vaccine production, active pharmaceutical ingredients (API), medical devices, clinical trials, and related pharmaceutical subsectors. It brought together 146 Chinese companies with around 220 delegates and more than 200 Pakistani firms, marking one of the largest China-Pakistan business engagements in the pharmaceutical, healthcare, and biotechnology sectors.
Federal Health Minister Mustafa Kamal announced on July 18 that 16 contracts and 80 memoranda of understanding had been finalized during the event. He termed the development a key economic milestone for cooperation between China and Pakistan in the pharmaceutical sector. The deals signed and the scope of the expected cooperation mark a clear shift toward industrial collaboration between the two countries, beyond the limited trade exchanges of earlier years.
Notably, Pakistan’s dependence on imported vaccines and pharmaceutical inputs remains critical. For instance, the country administers 13 vaccines under its national immunization program, and all these vaccines are imported. Moreover, while Pakistan manufactures about 85 percent of its finished medicines locally, it imports around 95 percent of the API required to produce them. The country’s dependency also extends to imports for essential vaccines and specialized medicines. This essentially means that Pakistan’s healthcare system is vulnerable to global shipping delays, currency shifts, cuts in foreign aid, and changes in donors’ priorities.
For its 240 million people, the consequences of vaccine import dependency are huge.
For instance, vaccine-preventable diseases, such as measles, diphtheria, polio, and rabies continue to affect people, especially children. At times, shortages and delayed shipments force health authorities to ration doses or postpone campaigns. In other cases, thousands of children die every year in Pakistan simply due to non-vaccination because their parents do not pay any heed to the importance of immunization. In this context, a lack of awareness and persistent vaccine shortages highlight a long-standing challenge within Pakistan’s pharmaceutical sector.
The government, it seems, is now pursuing broader pharmaceutical reforms with Chinese support to open an industry that has remained underdeveloped for a long time.
For the first time, Pakistan has approved a National Local Vaccine Production Policy. Arguably, the policy has set the framework for domestic vaccine manufacturing with assistance from Chinese companies. The policy seeks to build local production capacity, strengthen health security, and cut dependence on imported medicines and vaccines.
In this regard, the Chinese investment and technology transfer that is envisaged under the recent agreements could reshape the pharma sector. This is the first time that such substantial investment pledges and private-sector collaboration are happening with full support from the governments of both countries.
Pakistan is facing recurrent vaccine shortages and systemic challenges that severely undermine its immunization efforts. The economic costs of importing medicines intensify these challenges. Pakistan’s medicine and vaccine import costs run into hundreds of millions of dollars each year. It is estimated that the annual bill for imported vaccines could reach $1.2 billion by 2030. The planned local production could help Pakistan reduce imports and save foreign exchange.
Moreover, agreements have been reached with Chinese companies to produce raw materials domestically, which would further lower medicine prices and benefit the Pakistani public.
No other country apart from China has shown this level of interest in Pakistan’s pharmaceutical sector. Agreements signed at the conference include two in API manufacturing, eight in vaccine production, two in clinical trials, two in generic formulation injectables, and eight in medical devices. This could dramatically change Pakistan’s healthcare sector if implemented fully.
The deals struck recently pave the way for local production and knowledge transfer in the coming years.
As part of the agreements, Chinese firms are set to establish plants in Pakistan through joint ventures, co-produce raw materials, and build new industrial capacity that will also create jobs locally. Many of these units are expected to be built in special economic zones that are being developed under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor, where targeted policy incentives are expected to accelerate industrial growth.
That said, Chinese private investors might still face regulatory and other obstacles in research and development. The Pakistani government must provide a competitive and transparent environment that is free from political instability and regulatory confusion if the partnership is to deliver results. An opportunity like this may not come again and should be taken seriously by the federal government.

articles.title: Kashagan Environmental Fine Enforced in Kazakhstan
articles.full_text:
An asset freeze could be the first step of an acrimonious fight with the foreign oil majors developing one of the country’s largest oil fields.
Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Justice imposed a freeze on property and transport assets owned by the North Caspian Operating Company (NCOC), which is developing one of the country’s largest oil fields, over failure to pay a massive environmental fine.
The decision followed a back-and-forth between the government and NCOC, a collection of international oil companies drilling for oil at Kashagan, an offshore field in the Caspian Sea.
The July 21 decision was disclosed only three days later, and it remains unclear exactly what kind of property or transport assets were affected.
Also on July 21, according to Reuters sources, Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Justice told NCOC’s managing director Giancarlo Ruiu that he would be held responsible for “administrative and criminal liability for non-compliance.”
In 2023, a local court imposed a 2.3 trillion tenge ($4.9 billion) fine for improper sulfur storage on the consortium.
The fine, alongside a dispute over a number of provisions in the contract between the government and NCOC, became a bone of contention within much larger arbitration proceedings. 
Kazakhstan’s government claims that the conditions of the Kashagan contract are unfair and is now asking for a recalculation of the costs and a higher share of the profits. The claim, according to sources familiar with the arbitration proceedings, is worth around $165 billion.
On July 20, Kazakhstan’s Kazmunaigas, which owns 16.88 percent of NCOC, offered to pay its part of the environmental fine, insiders told Bloomberg.
The international partners in the consortium, meanwhile, refused. Shell, Eni, TotalEnergies, and ExxonMobil each hold a 16.81 percent stake, while China’s CNPC (8.33 percent) and Japan’s Inpex (7.65 percent) own the rest.
Given the complex and lengthy legal dispute, a UNCITRAL tribunal rejected Kazakhstan’s request to lift restraining measures on the enforcement of the environmental fine, which are in place as long as the arbitration between the parties remains pending.
Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Justice replied that the United Nations tribunal cannot limit its sovereign rights to enforce the fine.
“An interim order in a commercial arbitration proceeding under UNCITRAL rules does not have automatic effect in Kazakhstan and does not limit the state’s exercise of its sovereign powers to protect the environment and public interests,” an official note said.
Under Kazakhstan’s new Constitution, hastily approved via referendum on March 15 and in force since July 1, domestic laws have precedence over international obligations.
The foreign companies, meanwhile, said that they “consider the sulfur fine to be without any basis and are contesting it by all available means.”
In 2022, Kazakhstan levied a fine alleging that NCOC had breached its sulfur storage permits. Sulfur is a toxic byproduct of oil extraction and can be used as a component for fertilizers. NCOC sells most of its sulfur to Chinese importers, but a temporary ban on exports led to excessive amounts being stored in addition to the existing stockpile in the summer of 2022.
In the past, environmental fines have been used by the government of Kazakhstan to push for better conditions or a revision of existing agreements. Analysts argued that these fines are, in fact, political tools. 
In 2011, Kazakhstan’s government threatened an environmental fine against Karachaganak, a major gas and condensate field. The consortium sold off a 10 percent stake to Kazmunaigas and the fine disappeared. Seven years later, the foreign consortium operating Karachaganak agreed to pay Kazakhstan a $1.1 billion compensation to end all existing disputes. And yet, in January 2026, the government once again knocked at Karachaganak’s door and asked for an additional $4 billion.
The Kashagan deal was struck in 1997 and further amended in 2008. The contract, much like the one signed for Karachaganak, is a so-called production sharing agreement (PSA), which legal experts deem favorable toward private investors. 
According to the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists, Kazakhstan’s 2023 arbitral claim stated that NCOC “currently receives 98 percent of all post-Priority Payment revenue from oil production”
Kazakhstan’s President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev repeatedly urged the government to renegotiate better terms for the PSA and joint venture contracts that concern the largest oil fields. 
According to analysts, there are ongoing talks of contract overhauls for the three largest oil fields, including Tengiz and Karachaganak. Together, these fields produce the vast majority of Kazakhstan’s oil and represent major tax and hard currency contributors to the country’s budget.

articles.title: Why Australia Struggles to Foster Asia Experts
articles.full_text:
A new government report looks at Australia’s “Asia capability” and finds the country wanting.
Earlier this month, the Australian government published an inquiry into the development of the country’s Asia capability titled “Security and Prosperity in Asia: Building Asia Capability in Australia through the Education System and Beyond.” The capability this inquiry sought to evaluate includes the teaching and learning of Asian languages and cultures, alongside how best to facilitate the public’s broader regional engagement. 
The report argued that Australia’s prosperity, diplomacy, and strategic independence increasingly depend on Australians developing stronger knowledge of the Asian region; yet the institutions responsible for building this capability are weakening. Without a public who have a good ability to understand and engage effectively with Asia, there is a diminished capacity for Australia to advance itself and secure its future. 
The report distinguished between general Asia literacy for the broader population and the deeper specialist expertise required for diplomats, researchers, business leaders, defense officials, and policymakers. Yet the former feeds into the latter. Without a high baseline of knowledge within the general public, it is more difficult for the country to produce the critical mass of experts required to do the specialist roles. Schools should provide all students with a strong general knowledge of the region, and then universities can hone this into producing highly skilled experts with advanced knowledge. 
The report highlighted that this pipeline is exhibiting serious problems. It presented evidence that fewer Australians are studying Asian languages than in previous decades, particularly in languages deemed to be the priority for the Australian government – Indonesian, Japanese, and Mandarin. These have fallen sharply in secondary schools, and declined dramatically at universities. 
The study of Indonesian was singled out as facing a crisis. Indonesia is Australia’s largest near neighbor, so strategically it should be considered a vital subject. Yet the report described study of the Indonesian language as approaching “functional extinction” within the education systems of some states. 
This decline risks having a compounding effect. With fewer students studying Asian languages at school, universities will reduce or close language programs due to low demand. This then diminishes the number of future teachers, academics, and researchers required to sustain the system. The report warned that Australia risks losing the institutional capacity to build the Asia expertise it requires. 
There are some structural hurdles that Australia faces. The first is that responsibility of building Asia capabilities is fragmented across schools, universities, state governments, federal departments, and businesses. Because no single institution oversees the system as a whole, there is little coordination between school language programs, university pathways, workforce needs, and national strategic priorities. 
Despite the report being chaired by a government MP, former Assistant Minister for Foreign Affairs Tim Watts, the report highlighted the absence of national leadership from the federal government. 
The other structural hurdles are cultural, and this has two components. First, there is a deep complacency within the Australian psyche that restricts the country from investing in key capacities. It has long been identified that Australia has prospered from luck rather than effort, and this has bred an ingrained lethargic culture that prevents the country from engaging in foresight and preparedness. 
The second cultural problem is one of suspicion toward the region. While Australia has become a highly multicultural society and this has created strong diaspora links within Asia, there remains a cohort of people in the country who do not see the merit in developing greater cultural knowledge of the region and often see this as a threat. The current rise of the One Nation party especially can be viewed as a revolt against the country’s geography. 
Yet the thing about geography is that it cannot be changed. Mature countries understand their geographic positions and seek to take advantage of them. Australia’s run of extraordinary luck hasn’t ended, as the world’s economic center of gravity has shifted to the Indo-Pacific. That provides the country with a wealth of opportunities should it develop the skills to harness them. 
The report argued that advances in AI or translation technology are no solution, that instead these are lazy ways to address the capability deficit. These digital tools are unable to replace deeper cultural understanding, contextual knowledge, and the human relationships necessary for diplomacy, economic opportunity, and broader regional engagement. 
For once, Australians may be required to do some actual work. The report offered 34 recommendations that can create a path forward for Australia to enhance its Asia capabilities. These fall short of making priority languages compulsory school subjects, but they do present a blueprint for improvements. Yet these recommendations may still be futile if Australia cannot confront its own cultural resistance and lack of political will.

articles.title: Asia’s Overlooked Maritime Flashpoints
articles.full_text:
Besides the South China Sea, there are various waterways under contention, from open ocean to marshlands and rivers.
Sir Creek and the India-Pakistan coastal borderlands.
You’ve probably heard of the South China Sea disputes – a major flashpoint involving China, the Philippines, Vietnam, and others. But the South China Sea isn’t the only maritime dispute in Asia. 
Today, we’re going to talk about four often-overlooked maritime flashpoints in South and Southeast Asia – and how they’re reshaping the geopolitical landscape today. 
In East Asia, various states are mostly fighting over who owns particular rocks in order to claim control of the surrounding ocean. Things are different in South and Southeast Asia. Besides the South China Sea, there are various waterways under contention, from open ocean to marshlands and rivers. Even settled maritime borders are becoming problems thanks to changing political circumstances on the water and on land.
But which of these maritime flashpoints are most likely to lead to an actual conflict? Let’s dive in.
